drill.title: Bridge and claw grips on soft foods
body: Two grips keep your fingers safe on everything you'll cut in this unit. Practice them today on soft foods with a paring knife, slowly, until they feel natural. An adult is nearby the whole time.
steps: Lay a damp paper towel under the cutting board so it can't slide.
The bridge: set a banana on the board. Make a bridge over it with your hand, thumb on one side and fingers on the other.
Put the paring knife under the bridge and cut the banana in half. The blade never goes near your fingers.
The claw: lay one half flat side down. Curl your fingertips under and rest your knuckles against the side of the blade.
Slice the banana, moving your claw hand back a small step after each cut.
Do the same with a cucumber: bridge to halve it the long way, then claw to slice it into half-moons.
Slice 5 strawberries with the claw grip.
Set the knife down flat at the top of the board, blade away. Eat your practice, or save it for a snack.

quiz.q: When do you use the bridge grip?
choices: To cut something round in half
quiz.explain: The knife goes under the bridge.

quiz.q: In the claw grip, what guides the blade?
Why cut a cucumber in half before slicing it?
choices: So it lies flat and can't roll
quiz.explain: A flat side down holds still.

knowledge.title: Knife rules: grip, direction, where to set it down
body: A knife is safe when you follow a few rules every time, the same way every time. They're simple, and they matter more than speed.
Grip: hold the handle firmly, with all your fingers wrapped around it. Your other hand holds the food in a bridge or a claw, never flat in front of the blade.
Direction: cut down and away from you, toward the board. Never cut toward your hand, your body, or something you're holding in the air.

Where it goes: when you stop cutting, even for a moment, lay the knife flat at the top of the board with the blade facing away. Never leave it at the edge of the counter, under a towel or food, or in a sink of soapy water, where someone can't see it.
If it falls: step back and let it fall. Never try to catch a falling knife.
Carry and wash: carry a knife by the handle, point down, at your side. Wash it on its own, holding the handle, blade away from you, and dry it right away.

quiz.q: Which way do you cut?
choices: Down and away, toward the board

quiz.q: Where does the knife go when you stop cutting?
choices: Flat at the top of the board, blade away
At the edge of the counter

quiz.q: A knife falls off the counter. What do you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall

quiz.q: Why not put a knife in a sink of soapy water?
choices: Someone could reach in and not see it
quiz.explain: Wash it on its own instead.

quiz.q: How do you carry a knife?
choices: By the handle, point down, at your side
quiz.explain: So it points at no one.

sabbath.title: Wash and cut vegetables ahead for the week
body: A few minutes washing and cutting fruit and vegetables on one day saves time all week, and makes a healthy snack the easy choice.

Some keep well washed and cut: bell pepper strips, snap peas, and washed lettuce last 3 to 5 days in the fridge. Others are best cut on the day: tomatoes go mealy, and cucumbers go soft. Rinse berries just before you eat them, or they turn mushy.
A folded paper towel in the container soaks up extra water, which is what makes cut vegetables slimy.
steps: With an adult, pick two or three vegetables your family eats as snacks or in lunches.
Wash them, and dry them well with a towel or paper towels.
Cut the soft ones with the paring knife, using the bridge and the claw. Leave hard vegetables like carrots whole for now.
Line each container with a folded paper towel and pack one vegetable in each.
Label each with what it is and today's date, and put them in the fridge.
Check them in 3 days: which kept best?

quiz.q: Why put a paper towel in the container?
Which is best cut on the day you eat it?
When should berries be rinsed?

drill.title: Mitts on; handles in; pull out an oven rack safely
body: Today you'll practice three habits until they're automatic: mitts on, handles in, and a rack pulled out before the pan is lifted. Start with a cold oven, then do it again with the oven warm. An adult is beside you.
steps: Check your oven mitts are dry. Put one on each hand.
Set an empty pot on each burner of the cold stove. Turn every handle in, so none sticks out past the edge.
Walk past the stove and check: could your hip or sleeve catch a handle?
With the oven cold, move a rack to the middle. Put an empty sheet pan on it.
Mitts on: open the door, pull the rack out partway, lift the pan straight up, and set it on the stovetop. Push the rack in and close the door.
Now heat the oven to 200°F. When it's hot, do step 5 again, slowly.
Turn off the oven. Leave the pan on the stovetop until it's cool to the touch.

quiz.q: Which way do pot handles point?
Why pull the rack out before lifting the pan?
choices: So your arms stay away from the hot oven walls

quiz.q: Why must mitts be dry?
choices: Heat goes through wet cloth as steam
quiz.explain: A damp mitt burns in a second.

knowledge.title: Burns and scalds; a lid on a pan fire, never water
body: Most kitchen burns come from things you can see coming: a pot handle sticking out, a wet oven mitt, steam from a lid, or a splash of hot oil. A burn is from something hot and dry; a scald is from hot liquid or steam.

If you get a small burn: hold it under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, and tell an adult. Don't use ice, butter, or toothpaste. They trap the heat or damage the skin. A burn that's large, blistered, or on the face or hands needs an adult right away, and maybe a doctor.

A pan fire is usually oil that got too hot. Never throw water on it: water hits burning oil and explodes it into a ball of flame. Instead, an adult turns off the burner and slides a lid over the pan, which takes away the air the fire needs. Leave the lid on until the pan is cold. Never carry a burning pan.
An oven fire: keep the door closed and turn the oven off. The fire runs out of air. If any fire doesn't go out right away, everyone leaves the house and calls 911.

quiz.q: What do you do for a small burn?
choices: Cool running water for at least 10 minutes

quiz.q: Why never put water on a pan fire?
choices: It explodes the burning oil into flame
quiz.explain: Water and hot oil don't mix.

quiz.q: How do you put out a pan fire?
choices: Turn off the burner and slide a lid over the pan

quiz.q: Something's burning in the oven. What do you do?
choices: Keep the door closed and turn the oven off
quiz.explain: Opening it feeds the fire air.

quiz.q: What's a scald?
choices: A burn from hot liquid or steam
A burn from a dry pan
quiz.explain: Steam from a lid is a common one.

sabbath.title: Make a pot of soup ahead and reheat it
body: Soup is one of the best foods to make ahead. Many soups taste even better the next day.
The safe way to keep it: cool the soup within 2 hours of cooking. Pour it into shallow containers, no more than 2 inches deep, so it cools fast in the fridge. It keeps 3 to 4 days.
To reheat, warm it in a pot over medium heat, stirring, until it's steaming all the way through and bubbling at the edges. Only reheat what you'll eat, and reheat it once.
steps: Make this week's tomato soup, or a pot of soup with an adult.
Let it cool on the stovetop for no more than 30 minutes, lid off.
Ladle it into shallow containers. Label each with the soup's name and the date.
Put them in the fridge, uncovered until cold, then cover them.
Later in the week, reheat one container in a pot until steaming, stirring often.
Taste it: does it taste the same as the first day?

quiz.q: How soon should cooked soup go in the fridge?
quiz.explain: Then germs don't have time to grow.

quiz.q: Why shallow containers?
How hot should reheated soup be?

drill.title: Set out a recipe's mise en place in small bowls; clean as you go
body: Mise en place, French for "everything in its place," means setting out every ingredient and tool before you start cooking. Today you'll practice it with this week's recipe, and clean as you go.
steps: Read this week's recipe all the way through.
Set out every tool it needs on the counter.
Measure each ingredient into its own small bowl or cup. Line the bowls up in the order the recipe uses them.
Put each package or jar away as soon as you've measured from it.
Wipe the counter and the board before you start cooking.
Cook the recipe. Each time you wait, wash a dish or put something away.
When you finish: is the kitchen clean, or nearly?

quiz.q: What does mise en place mean?
When does a package go back in the cupboard?
choices: As soon as you've measured from it

quiz.q: What can you do while food cooks?
choices: Wash a dish or put something away

knowledge.title: Parts of a recipe: yield, ingredients, steps, abbreviations
body: Every recipe is written in the same parts. Knowing them means you can read any recipe, from any book or website.
The title and the yield come first. The yield says how much it makes: "Serves 4" or "Makes 12." The time tells you how long it takes, start to finish.

The ingredients are listed in the order you use them. Watch the words after each one: "1 cup onion, chopped" means measure, then chop. "1 cup chopped onion" means chop, then measure. They're different amounts.
The steps say what to do, in order. Read them all before you start, so nothing surprises you.

Recipes shorten common words: tsp or t is teaspoon; tbsp or T is tablespoon (3 teaspoons); c is cup; oz is ounce; lb is pound; fl oz is fluid ounce, for liquids; pkg is package; and °F is degrees Fahrenheit.

quiz.q: What does the yield tell you?
What does tbsp mean?
quiz.explain: A big T is a tablespoon too.

quiz.q: How many teaspoons are in a tablespoon?
"1 cup onion, chopped" means:
choices: Use a cup of any onion
quiz.explain: The comma means do it after measuring.

quiz.q: Why read the whole recipe before you start?

sabbath.title: Gleaning: Ruth in the fields (Ruth 2)
body: God's law built care for the poor into the harvest. Farmers were told not to cut the grain at the very edges of their fields, and not to go back for what they dropped. What was left was for the poor and for foreigners to gather (Leviticus 19:9–10). Gathering it is called gleaning.

Ruth was a widow from Moab who came to Bethlehem with her mother-in-law, Naomi, who was poor. Ruth went to glean barley in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's. Boaz told his workers to let her glean freely, and even to pull some stalks out of the bundles on purpose for her (Ruth 2:15–16). By evening she had enough barley to feed them both.
Gleaning let people work for their own food, and let farmers give by leaving, not only by handing out.
steps: Read Ruth 2 with an adult.
Answer out loud or in writing: who was the gleaning for?
Answer: what did Boaz do that was more than the law asked?
With your family, choose one way to "leave the edges" this week, like making extra of a meal for someone, or giving food to a food bank.
Write it down, and do it if you can.

quiz.q: What is gleaning?
choices: Gathering what's left in a field after the harvest
quiz.explain: It was left for the poor.

quiz.q: Whose field did Ruth glean in?
What did Boaz tell his workers to do?
choices: Pull out stalks on purpose for Ruth

drill.title: Measure dry vs. wet; level a cup
body: Dry and wet ingredients are measured in different cups, in different ways. Today you'll learn both and see why it matters.
steps: Dry: spoon flour into a dry measuring cup until it's heaped. Don't press or shake it.
Sweep the flat side of a table knife across the top to level it. That's 1 cup.
Now scoop a cup of flour straight from the bag and press it down. Compare the two cups on a kitchen scale, if you have one.
Wet: set the liquid measuring cup on the counter. Pour in water to the 1-cup line.
Bend down so your eyes are level with the line. Is it exactly on it?
Spoons: fill a teaspoon with salt and level it with the knife. Do the same with a tablespoon.
Pour the flour back, and wipe up.

quiz.q: How do you measure flour?
choices: Spoon it in loosely and level it

quiz.q: How do you read a liquid measuring cup?
choices: At eye level, on the counter

quiz.q: What levels a measuring cup or spoon?
choices: The flat side of a table knife

knowledge.title: Halving and doubling a recipe
body: A recipe makes a set amount, but your family might need more or less. Halving means using half of every amount. Doubling means using two times every amount.
Some amounts are easy: 1 cup doubled is 2 cups; 1 cup halved is ½ cup. Others need a conversion. It helps to know: 3 teaspoons = 1 tablespoon; 4 tablespoons = ¼ cup; 16 tablespoons = 1 cup.
So half of 1 tablespoon is 1½ teaspoons. Half of ¼ cup is 2 tablespoons. Half of ⅓ cup is 2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons.
Half an egg: beat one egg in a cup and use half of it, about 2 tablespoons.

Some things don't change the same way. Cooking time stays about the same when you double: 8 pizzas take as long to bake as 4, as long as they fit on the pans. A bigger batch may need a bigger pot or two pans. Write your new amounts down before you start.

quiz.q: How many tablespoons in ¼ cup?
What's half of 1 tablespoon?
You double a pizza recipe. How long do they bake?
quiz.explain: If they fit on the pans.

quiz.q: How do you use half an egg?
choices: Beat it and use about half

quiz.q: When do you write down the new amounts?

sabbath.title: Make a dip ahead and store it covered
body: A dip made ahead is a ready snack all week, with vegetables, pita chips, or crackers. This one needs no cooking, only measuring and stirring.
Yogurt dip keeps covered in the fridge for up to 3 days. Stir it before serving, since a little liquid may rise to the top.
steps: Measure 1 cup of plain Greek yogurt into a bowl. Check its label for gelatin first.
Add 1 tablespoon of lemon juice, ½ teaspoon of jarred minced garlic, 1 teaspoon of dried dill, and ¼ teaspoon of salt.
Stir until smooth. Taste, and add a pinch more salt if it needs it.
Spoon it into a container with a lid. Label it with the date.
Put it in the fridge. Use it within 3 days.
For practice, work out what you'd use for a double batch, and write it down.

quiz.q: How long does the dip keep in the fridge?
Doubling the dip, how much yogurt?
Why check the yogurt's label?
quiz.explain: Gelatin can come from unclean animals.

drill.title: Peel, core, and seed a cucumber and a tomato
body: Peeling, coring, and seeding take the tough or watery parts out of a vegetable before it goes in a salad. Today you'll do all three with a peeler, a paring knife, and a spoon. An adult is nearby.
steps: Lay a damp paper towel under the cutting board. Rinse a cucumber and a tomato.
Hold the cucumber by one end on the board. Peel it in long strokes away from you, turning it as you go.
Trim both ends with the paring knife. Cut it in half the long way, using the bridge grip.
Scrape the seeds out of each half with the tip of a spoon.
Cut the tomato in half through the stem. Cut a small V around the stem in each half to take out the core.
Scoop out the tomato's seeds with the spoon.
Slice the cucumber halves into half-moons and the tomato into wedges. Eat them as a snack, or use them in this week's recipe today.

quiz.q: Which way do you pull the peeler?
quiz.explain: The blade never comes toward your body.

quiz.q: What scoops out the seeds?
quiz.explain: A spoon follows the curve without cutting.

quiz.q: What is the core of a tomato?
choices: The hard part under the stem
quiz.explain: Cut it out with a small V.

knowledge.title: Washing produce: what to wash and what not to
body: Fruits and vegetables can carry dirt and germs from the field, the truck, and the store. Rinsing them under cool running water just before you use them washes most of it away.
Wash: anything you'll eat raw, and anything you'll cut, even if you won't eat the peel. A knife going through a melon, an avocado, or an orange carries whatever is on the skin into the part you eat.

How: rub produce with your hands under running water. Scrub firm things like potatoes and carrots with a clean brush. Pull lettuce leaves apart and rinse each one. Then dry them with a clean towel or paper towel. No soap, bleach, or produce wash: plain water works, and soap can soak into food.
When: right before you use it, not when you put it away. Washed produce stored wet spoils faster.

Don't wash: bagged greens marked "ready to eat" or "triple washed" (rinsing them in a dirty sink can add germs), raw chicken or meat (the splashes spread germs across the kitchen), and eggs (they're cleaned before they're sold).
steps: Look in your fridge with an adult. Find two things to wash before eating and one bag marked ready to eat.
Wash one fruit or vegetable the right way, rubbing it under running water, and dry it.

quiz.q: When do you wash produce?
choices: As soon as you get home

quiz.q: Why wash a melon if you don't eat the rind?
choices: The knife carries germs from the rind inside
quiz.explain: Whatever is on the skin goes in with the knife.

quiz.q: What do you wash produce with?
Which should you not wash?
quiz.explain: Splashes spread germs around the kitchen.

sabbath.title: Daily bread (Matthew 6:11)
body: When Jesus taught His followers to pray, one of the things He told them to ask for was food: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). Not a year's worth, or a week's: today's.

In the wilderness, God fed Israel with manna one day at a time (Exodus 16:4). Proverbs asks God for "neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me" (Proverbs 30:8). And later in the same chapter of Matthew, Jesus tells His followers not to worry about what they'll eat, because their Father knows they need it (Matthew 6:31–33).
Asking for daily bread is a way of remembering that every meal is a gift, and of trusting God for tomorrow's.
steps: Read Matthew 6:9–13 with an adult.
Read Matthew 6:25–33.
Answer out loud or in writing: why do you think Jesus said "this day" and not "this year"?
List five foods your family ate this week. Next to each, write one person who helped bring it to your table: a farmer, a driver, a cook.
Before a meal this week, thank God for that day's food.

quiz.q: In the Lord's Prayer, what bread do we ask for?
How often did God send manna?
In Matthew 6, why don't we need to worry about food?
choices: Our Father knows we need it

drill.title: Whisk a vinaigrette, taste it, and fix it
body: A vinaigrette is oil, vinegar, and salt whisked together. Today you'll make a small one, taste it, and fix it, one change at a time.
steps: In a small bowl, put 1 tablespoon of vinegar, a pinch of salt, and ½ teaspoon of mustard. Whisk until the salt dissolves.
Keep whisking while you pour in 3 tablespoons of olive oil, a little at a time.
Dip a piece of lettuce or cucumber in it and taste.
Too sour? Whisk in 1 teaspoon of oil. Flat? Add a pinch of salt. Oily? Add a few drops of vinegar.
Taste again after each change. Write down what you changed.
Use it on a salad today, or keep it in a jar in the fridge for up to a week.

quiz.q: Why change only one thing at a time?
choices: So you know which change helped
quiz.explain: Two at once, and you can't tell.

quiz.q: The dressing tastes oily and flat. What do you add?
choices: Salt or a few drops of vinegar
quiz.explain: Salt and sour wake it up.

knowledge.title: Oil and vinegar: why a dressing separates
body: Oil and vinegar don't mix. Vinegar is mostly water, and oil and water push apart. Whisk them and the oil breaks into tiny drops spread through the vinegar, so the dressing looks cloudy. Leave it, and the drops join back together and float to the top.
That's why a dressing separates in the jar. It's not spoiled: whisk or shake it again right before you pour it.

Some things help a dressing stay mixed longer. Mustard and mayonnaise hold onto oil and water at the same time, so they keep the drops apart. That's why Caesar dressing, made with mayonnaise, stays creamy, and a vinaigrette with mustard stays mixed longer than one without.
A good starting mix is 3 spoons of oil to 1 spoon of vinegar or lemon juice, with a pinch of salt. Then taste it on a piece of what you're dressing, and change it to suit you.
steps: Put 1 tablespoon of vinegar and 3 tablespoons of oil in a clean jar with a lid. Shake it hard and watch: how long until it separates?
Add ½ teaspoon of mustard, shake again, and time it. What changed?

quiz.q: Why does a dressing separate?
What helps a dressing stay mixed?
quiz.explain: They hold onto oil and water at the same time.

quiz.q: What's a good starting mix?
choices: 3 spoons of oil to 1 of vinegar
1 spoon of oil to 3 of vinegar

quiz.q: The dressing separated in the jar. What do you do?

sabbath.title: Pack a lunch salad with the dressing apart
body: A salad packed for lunch stays crisp if the dressing travels on its own. Dressing on lettuce for hours makes it limp and watery.

Pack sturdy things on the bottom and leaves on top, and carry the dressing in a small container with a tight lid. Pour and toss right before you eat. Keep it cold: a lunch with chicken, cheese, or mayonnaise needs an ice pack, or a fridge, until lunchtime.
steps: Make a small jar of this week's vinaigrette or Caesar dressing.
In a container, put sturdy things first: chickpeas, cucumber, or chicken.
Put lettuce on top. Close the lid.
Spoon dressing into a small container with a tight lid. Label both with the date.
Keep them in the fridge, and pack them with an ice pack for lunch.
At lunch, pour, close the lid, and shake to toss. How crisp is it?

quiz.q: Why pack the dressing apart?
What goes on the bottom of the container?
quiz.explain: Leaves go on top, away from the wet.

quiz.q: What keeps a lunch with chicken safe?
choices: An ice pack or a fridge
quiz.explain: Keep it cold until you eat.

drill.title: Read a thermometer; check a patty for 160°F
body: A thermometer is the only way to know ground beef is safe. Today you'll practice reading one, then use it on a real patty. An adult is in the kitchen while the stove is on.
steps: Find the thermometer's probe, the metal stick, and its tip, which is where it reads. Turn it on, or wait for the dial to settle.
Fill a glass with ice and water. Put the tip in the middle of the glass for 30 seconds. It should read about 32°F.
Hold the tip under warm tap water, then cold. Watch how long the number takes to stop moving.
Shape a small beef patty, wash your hands, and cook it in a skillet over medium heat, 3 minutes a side.
Slide the thermometer into the side of the patty so the tip is in the middle. Wait for the number to stop moving.
If it reads 160°F or more, it's done. If not, cook it 1 more minute and check again.
Wash the probe with hot, soapy water. Write down what your patty read.

quiz.q: Where does a thermometer read?
quiz.explain: Put the tip in the middle of the food.

quiz.q: What should it read in ice water?
When do you read the number?
choices: After a minute out of the food
quiz.explain: It takes a few seconds to settle.

knowledge.title: Why ground meat must reach 160°F
body: Germs that can make people sick live on the outside of meat. When beef is ground, the outside gets mixed all the way through, so germs can be in the middle of a burger too.
Heat kills those germs. At 160°F, ground beef is safe. You can't tell by color: beef can turn brown inside before it's safe, or stay a little pink after it is. Only a thermometer can tell you.
Every kind of meat has its own safe temperature. You'll learn chicken's (165°F) and fish's (145°F) later in this unit.
steps: Make a small card that says "Ground beef: 160°F" and keep it by the stove.
Ask an adult what temperature they cook burgers to. Tell them what you learned.

quiz.q: Why do germs end up in the middle of a burger?
choices: Grinding mixes the outside all through

quiz.q: What temperature makes ground beef safe?
Can you tell a burger is done by its color?
choices: No, only a thermometer can tell

sabbath.title: Shape patties ahead and freeze them
body: Shaped patties freeze well. With a stack in the freezer, burgers or köfte are ready to cook any night, with the messy raw-meat part already done.
steps: Shape ground beef into patties, the same size as this week's recipe. Wash your hands after.
Lay them on a parchment-lined plate or sheet pan, not touching, and freeze them for 1 hour.
Stack the frozen patties with a square of parchment between each one, and put them in a freezer bag.
Press out the air, seal it, and write the date and "ground beef" on the bag.
Use them within 3 months. Thaw them in the fridge overnight, then cook them to 160°F as usual.
Wash your hands, and wipe everything the raw beef touched.

quiz.q: Why freeze the patties apart first?
choices: So they don't freeze stuck together
quiz.explain: Then they stack and come apart easily.

quiz.q: Where do frozen patties thaw?
What goes on the bag?
quiz.explain: So you know what it is and how old.

drill.title: Read 10 labels and find the hidden unclean ingredients
body: Some foods hide ingredients that aren't clean. Today you'll read real labels and find them, using the watch-for list below and the longer one on this week's Knowledge page. Your family's kitchen and a grocery store both work.
steps: Pick 10 packaged foods: try yogurt, sour cream, tortillas, taco shells, refried beans, gummy candy, marshmallows, a seasoning packet, a sauce, and one of your choice.
Turn each one over and find the ingredient list.
Read the whole list, slowly. Look for the names on the watch-for list, and for animal fats that don't say which animal.
Sort them into three piles: clean, not clean, and not sure.
For each one in "not sure", write down the word that made you stop. Ask an adult to look it up with you.
Tell an adult which foods you'd pick and which you'd put back.

quiz.q: Where do you find what's really in a food?
Which of these can hide gelatin?
A label says only "animal fat." Is it clean?
choices: You can't tell, so pass on it

watch.name: Lard
watch.hides: In some tortillas, taco shells, and refried beans.

watch.name: Gelatin
watch.hides: In some yogurt, sour cream, gummy candy, and marshmallows.

watch.name: Carmine or cochineal
watch.hides: A red coloring in some yogurts, candies, and drinks.

knowledge.title: Hidden unclean ingredients and where they hide
body: Unclean foods don't always look like what they are. They can be one word on a long ingredient list, and some have names you wouldn't guess.
The list below names the ones to watch for and where they hide. Learn the names: they're what you'll see on the label.
Meat can hide too. Packages called "ground meat" or "meatloaf mix" can mix more than one animal. The label should name every animal.
The rule is simple: if the label doesn't tell you, or you can't tell what a word means, pass on it.
steps: Make a list of the six names on this page. Keep it on your phone or in your pocket for shopping.
Find one food at home with a hidden ingredient, and one that's clean.

quiz.q: What is gelatin usually made from?
choices: Pigs, unless the label says beef or fish

quiz.q: What should a ground beef label say?
quiz.explain: Mixed packages can hold other meats.

quiz.q: You can't tell what a word on the label means. What do you do?
choices: Pass on it, or look it up first

watch.name: Lard
watch.hides: Fat from pigs. Used in some tortillas, taco shells, refried beans, and pie crusts.

watch.name: Gelatin
watch.hides: Usually made from pigs, unless the label says beef or fish. In some yogurt, sour cream, gummy candy, and marshmallows.

watch.name: Pork casings
watch.hides: The skin around many chicken and turkey sausages. Look for collagen casings or skinless.

watch.name: Oyster sauce
watch.hides: Made from a sea animal with a shell. In many stir-fry sauces. Mushroom stir-fry sauce works instead.

watch.name: Shrimp paste
watch.hides: In many Thai curry pastes and some kimchi.

watch.name: Carmine or cochineal
watch.hides: A red coloring made from crushed bugs. In some yogurts, candies, and drinks.

sabbath.title: Clean and unclean animals (Leviticus 11:1–8)
body: God gave Israel a simple test for land animals: "Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat" (Leviticus 11:3). An animal has to pass both parts.
A split hoof is a hoof divided into two toes, like a cow's. Chewing the cud means bringing swallowed food back up to chew again. Cows, sheep, goats, and deer do both, so they're clean.

The next verses name animals that pass only one part. The camel, the rock badger, and the hare chew the cud but don't have split hooves, and the pig has split hooves but doesn't chew the cud (Leviticus 11:4–7). Passing one part isn't enough.
steps: Read Leviticus 11:1–8 with an adult.
Draw two circles that overlap. Label one "split hoof" and one "chews the cud."
Put each animal from the passage where it belongs. The clean ones go in the middle, where the circles overlap.
Add three animals you know (try a cow, a horse, and a deer) and decide where they go.
Answer out loud: why isn't one part of the test enough?

quiz.q: What are the two parts of the test for land animals?
choices: A split hoof and chewing the cud
Eating grass and living on a farm

quiz.q: Which of these is clean?
Why is the camel unclean?
choices: It chews the cud but doesn't have a split hoof

drill.title: Thaw frozen fish safely: in the fridge or in cold water
body: Most fish at the store is sold frozen, and it has to thaw before it cooks evenly. There are two safe ways, and one way that isn't. Today you'll try both safe ones on the frozen fish you bought for this week's recipe, so nothing extra is needed.
steps: Take this week's frozen fish and split it into two sealed zip-top bags, half in each.
The night before you cook, put one bag on a plate on the bottom shelf of the fridge. The plate catches any drips.
The next day, fill a big bowl with cold tap water. Put the other bag in it, pressed under the water.
Change the water every 30 minutes so it stays cold. Check the fish by pressing it through the bag.
When it's soft all the way through, it's thawed. Write down how long it took.
Compare the two halves. Both go into this week's recipe today.
Never thaw fish on the counter. Wash your hands, the plate, and the bowl after.

quiz.q: What are the two safe ways to thaw fish?
choices: In the fridge, or sealed in cold water
On the counter, or in the sun
In hot water, or on the stove

quiz.q: How often do you change the cold water?
Where does fish thaw in the fridge?
choices: On a plate on the bottom shelf

knowledge.title: Fins and scales: which fish are clean; reading fish labels
body: For animals in the water, the test is fins and scales: a water animal must have both to be clean (Leviticus 11:9). Salmon, cod, tilapia, tuna, trout, and many more are clean.

Some water animals are unclean: fish with smooth skin and no scales, every animal with a shell, and the soft sea animals with arms. The list below names the common ones. Swordfish is left out because people disagree about its scales.

Once fish is cut into a fillet, you can't see the scales, so the label matters. It must say what fish it is. If it only says "whitefish" or "seafood," or names a fish you don't know, ask what it is or pass on it. Some cheap white fillets, sold as swai or basa, come from a fish with no scales.
steps: Write down five clean fish from this page.
At the store with an adult, read the names on three fish packages. Are they clean?

quiz.q: What must a water animal have to be clean?
Which of these is clean?
quiz.explain: Monkfish and swai have no scales.

quiz.q: Why read the name on a fish fillet?
choices: You can't see the scales on a fillet
To know how to cook it
quiz.explain: The name tells you what fish it is.

watch.name: Catfish, monkfish, swai, and basa
watch.hides: Fins but no scales. Swai and basa are sold as cheap white fillets.

watch.name: Shrimp, crab, lobster, clams, oysters, mussels, and scallops
watch.hides: Animals with shells. Also in some seafood mixes, and imitation seafood sticks can include them.

watch.name: Squid, calamari, and octopus
watch.hides: The soft sea animals with arms. In some seafood mixes and fried appetizers.

sabbath.title: Fins and scales (Leviticus 11:9–12)
body: "These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat" (Leviticus 11:9).
The next verses say the rest are "detestable" for food (Leviticus 11:10–12). Deuteronomy says the same thing again (Deuteronomy 14:9–10).
Fish were everyday food in Bible times. Several of Jesus' disciples were fishermen on the Sea of Galilee, and after He rose, Jesus cooked fish for them on the shore (John 21:9–13).
steps: Read Leviticus 11:9–12 with an adult.
Read Deuteronomy 14:9–10. What's the same as Leviticus?
Look at a picture of a salmon or a trout. Point to its fins and its scales.
Read John 21:9–13. Draw the breakfast Jesus made.
Answer out loud: why do you think God gave the same rule twice?

quiz.q: What two things does Leviticus 11:9 say a water animal needs?
Where else is the same rule written?
What did Jesus cook on the shore in John 21?

drill.title: Separate boards and hand-washing for raw chicken
body: Raw chicken can carry germs that make people sick. Today you'll set up a raw-chicken spot in your kitchen and practice washing your hands the right way, so you're ready for this week's recipe on your own.
steps: Pick one cutting board for raw meat only. Put a piece of tape on it that says "raw".
Pick a spot on the counter near the sink for raw chicken. Clear everything else away from it.
Wash your hands: wet them, add soap, and scrub the backs, between your fingers, and under your nails for 20 seconds. Hum "Happy Birthday" twice.
Rinse and dry your hands on a clean towel or a paper towel.
Put a little flour on your hands, as if it were raw chicken. Touch the faucet, a drawer handle, and the fridge door.
See how far it spread? Wipe each spot with hot, soapy water, then wash your hands again.
From now on, wash those spots every time you touch raw chicken.

quiz.q: How long do you scrub with soap?
What did the flour show you?
choices: How far raw-chicken germs spread from your hands
quiz.explain: Everything you touch picks it up.

quiz.q: Which board does raw chicken go on?
quiz.explain: Only raw meat goes on it.

knowledge.title: Raw meat on the bottom shelf; 165°F for chicken
body: Raw chicken and meat go on the bottom shelf of the fridge, in a bowl or on a plate. If juice leaks out, it can't drip onto food that won't be cooked, like fruit or leftovers.

Chicken is safe at 165°F, a little higher than ground beef. Check the thickest piece, and check more than one, because some pieces are always bigger. Never rinse raw chicken: it splashes germs around the sink and doesn't clean it.
Cooked chicken goes on a clean plate, never the one that held it raw.
steps: Look in your fridge. Is there a bottom-shelf spot for raw meat? Clear one with an adult.
Add "Chicken: 165°F" to your temperature card from week 7.

quiz.q: Where does raw chicken go in the fridge?
choices: On the bottom shelf, on a plate
quiz.explain: So it can't drip on other food.

quiz.q: What temperature does chicken need?
Where does cooked chicken go?
choices: The plate it sat on raw
quiz.explain: Raw-chicken germs stay on that plate.

sabbath.title: Clean and unclean birds (Leviticus 11:13–19)
body: For birds, Leviticus doesn't give a test. It gives a list of birds not to eat (Leviticus 11:13–19). Most of them hunt other animals or eat dead ones: the eagle, the vultures, the hawk, the owls, the raven, the heron, and more. The bat is on the list too.

Every bird not on the list is clean (Deuteronomy 14:11). That includes chicken, turkey, duck, goose, and quail. When Israel was hungry in the wilderness, God sent quail for them to eat (Exodus 16:13).
steps: Read Leviticus 11:13–19 with an adult.
Pick three birds from the list. Find a picture of each and write what it eats.
Read Exodus 16:11–13. What did God send in the evening?
Make a list of the birds your family eats. Check each one against Leviticus 11:13–19.

quiz.q: How does Leviticus tell which birds aren't clean?
Which of these is clean?
What bird did God send Israel in the wilderness?

drill.title: Spoon and level flour; wet into dry, don't overmix
body: Two habits make muffins soft: measuring flour the right way, and stirring just enough. You'll practice both with the flour and milk this week's recipe already buys. An adult is at the stove with you.
steps: Push a measuring cup into the flour bag and level it. Tip it onto a plate.
Now spoon flour into the cup without pressing, and scrape it flat with a butter knife. Tip it onto a second plate.
Which pile is bigger? If you have a kitchen scale, weigh them both. The spooned cup is the right one.
In two small bowls, stir together 3 tablespoons of flour, ½ teaspoon of sugar, and ¼ teaspoon of baking powder.
Add 2 tablespoons of milk and 1 teaspoon of oil to each bowl.
Bowl 1: stir 8 times and stop, lumps and all. Bowl 2: stir hard for 1 minute, until smooth.
With an adult, cook each as a small pancake in an oiled skillet over medium heat. Flip when bubbles cover the top.
Tear each one open. Which is softer? Which is taller?

quiz.q: How do you measure flour?
choices: Spoon it into the cup and scrape it flat
Scoop the cup into the bag

quiz.q: Which pancake was softer?
quiz.explain: Lots of stirring makes it tough.

quiz.q: What does a lumpy muffin batter mean?
choices: You stopped at the right time

knowledge.title: Baking soda vs. baking powder
body: Muffins and quick breads rise without yeast. Baking soda or baking powder makes tiny bubbles of gas in the batter, and the oven sets the batter around them.
Baking soda needs something sour to work, like buttermilk, yogurt, brown sugar, or bananas. As soon as they meet, it starts to fizz. That's why a soda batter goes into the oven right away.

Baking powder is baking soda with a dry sour powder already mixed in. It works with plain milk, and it fizzes twice: once when it gets wet, and again when it gets hot. They look alike, so read the box.
steps: With an adult, put 2 tablespoons of vinegar in a glass. Stir in ¼ teaspoon of baking soda. Watch it fizz.
Put ¼ cup of warm tap water in a second glass. Stir in ½ teaspoon of baking powder. Does it fizz too?
Put ¼ cup of plain water in a third glass. Stir in ¼ teaspoon of baking soda. What happens? Why?
Look at this week's recipe. Which one does it use?

quiz.q: What does baking soda need to fizz?
choices: Something sour, like buttermilk or vinegar
quiz.explain: In plain water, it barely fizzes.

quiz.q: What is baking powder?
choices: Baking soda with a sour powder mixed in
quiz.explain: So it works with plain milk.

quiz.q: Why does a baking soda batter go in the oven right away?
choices: The bubbles start as soon as it's mixed
quiz.explain: Wait too long and the bubbles escape.

sabbath.title: Bake muffins ahead and freeze them
body: Muffins are best warm, and they freeze well. Bake a batch, freeze what you don't eat, and warm one up any morning in less than a minute.
steps: Let this week's muffins cool all the way on the rack, about 1 hour.
Put them in a freezer bag. Press out the air and close it.
Write the name and the date on the bag. They keep for 3 months.
To eat one, wrap it in a paper towel and microwave it for 30 seconds.
Try a warmed frozen muffin. Does it taste fresh?

quiz.q: Why cool muffins before freezing them?
choices: Warm ones steam in the bag and get soggy

quiz.q: How long do muffins keep in the freezer?
quiz.explain: Write the date on the bag.

quiz.q: How do you warm a frozen muffin?
choices: In a paper towel in the microwave, about 30 seconds

drill.title: Cut cold butter into flour
body: You'll cut cold butter into flour two ways and see the difference, then bake your practice into four little biscuits. Use the flour, butter, and buttermilk this week's recipe already buys.
steps: Cut 3 tablespoons of cold butter into small cubes with a butter knife. Chill them 10 minutes.
Put ½ cup of flour, ½ teaspoon of baking powder, and a pinch of salt in a bowl.
Add the butter. Press it into the flour with a fork until the pieces are the size of peas.
Take out 1 spoonful and look. Rub that spoonful between your fingertips until it's like sand. See the difference?
Put the spoonful back. Stir in 3 tablespoons of buttermilk with the fork, just until it comes together.
Drop 4 spoonfuls onto a lined sheet pan. With an adult, bake at 425°F for 12 minutes, until golden.
Pull one apart. Can you see the little pockets where the butter was?

quiz.q: How big should the butter pieces be for biscuits?
What do you cut the butter in with?
quiz.explain: Work fast, so it stays cold.

quiz.q: Why chill the butter cubes first?

knowledge.title: Why cold fat makes flaky layers
body: Flaky biscuits and pastry come from little pieces of cold butter. Butter is part water. In a hot oven, that water turns to steam, and the steam pushes the dough up into thin layers.

If the butter is warm, it smears into the flour, and there's no steam pocket. The biscuits come out flat and dense. So bakers keep the butter cold, work fast, and use their fingertips, which are cooler than their palms.
Rubbing the butter in very fine, like breadcrumbs, makes something tender but not flaky, like Welsh cakes. Leaving it in pieces the size of peas makes flaky layers, like biscuits.
steps: Pull apart one of this week's biscuits or Welsh cakes. Look at the inside.
Do you see layers or a soft crumb? Draw what you see.
Answer out loud: why does the butter need to stay cold?

quiz.q: What makes the flaky layers in biscuits?
quiz.explain: The steam pushes the layers apart.

quiz.q: What happens if the butter gets warm?
choices: It smears in and the biscuits come out flat

quiz.q: Why use your fingertips, not your palms?

sabbath.title: Manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16)
body: When Israel was in the wilderness, they were hungry. God sent bread from heaven, called manna. Every morning it lay on the ground like frost, and the people gathered it (Exodus 16:4, 14–15).

God gave a rule with it. Each family gathered just what they needed for that day. Manna kept until the next morning went bad. But on the sixth day, they gathered twice as much, and that manna kept for the seventh day, the Sabbath (Exodus 16:16–26).
Manna taught Israel to trust God for each day's food. It tasted "like wafers made with honey" (Exodus 16:31).
steps: Read Exodus 16:13–21 with an adult.
Read Exodus 16:22–26. What was different on the sixth day?
Read Exodus 16:31. Draw what you think manna looked like.
Answer out loud: what did gathering manna every morning teach the people?

quiz.q: What did God send Israel to eat each morning?
What happened to manna kept until the next morning?
choices: It went bad, except on the sixth day

quiz.q: What did manna taste like?

drill.title: Bloom yeast; knead for 5 minutes
body: Two yeast skills: blooming the yeast, and kneading for 5 minutes. You'll practice with a small dough from the flour and yeast this week's recipe already buys.
steps: Fill two cups with ¼ cup of water each: one cold from the tap, one 105 to 110°F. Check with the thermometer.
Stir a pinch of sugar and ½ teaspoon of yeast into each. Set a timer for 10 minutes.
Which one foamed? Pour the cold one out.
Stir ¾ cup of flour and a pinch of salt into the foamy cup's water in a bowl.
Flour the counter. Knead: push the dough away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, and turn it.
Set a timer for 5 minutes. Feel the dough at the start, the middle, and the end.
Is it smoother now? Poke it. Does it spring back?
Roll it flat and cook it in a dry skillet with an adult, or throw it out.

quiz.q: Which cup of yeast foamed?
How long do you knead at Level 2?
How does kneaded dough feel?
choices: Smooth, and a poke springs back

knowledge.title: What yeast does in a dough
body: Yeast is alive. It's a tiny living thing, too small to see one at a time. A packet holds millions of them, asleep and dry.
Warm water wakes them up. Then they eat the sugar in the dough and breathe out a gas called carbon dioxide. The gas makes bubbles, and the bubbles make the dough rise.
Kneading makes the dough stretchy, like a balloon, so it holds the gas in. Too hot, and the yeast dies. Too cold, and it works very slowly.
steps: With an adult, put ½ cup of warm water (105 to 110°F) in a small plastic bottle.
Add 1 teaspoon of sugar and 1 teaspoon of yeast. Swirl it.
Stretch a balloon over the top of the bottle.
Wait 20 minutes. What happened to the balloon? Why?

quiz.q: What is yeast?
quiz.explain: It wakes up in warm water.

quiz.q: What does yeast breathe out?
What happens if the water is too hot?

sabbath.title: Make dough ahead and chill it
body: Pizza and naan dough can be made a day or two ahead and kept in the fridge. The cold slows the yeast way down, so the dough rises very slowly. It even tastes better.
On baking day, the dough is ready to shape, and you skip the wait.
steps: Make this week's dough and knead it as the recipe says.
Rub a little oil in a zip-top bag or a container with a lid. Put the dough in and close it.
Write the name and the date on it. Put it in the fridge. It keeps 2 days.
On baking day, take it out 1 hour before you shape it, so it warms up.
Shape and bake it as the recipe says. Does it taste different?

quiz.q: What does the fridge do to yeast?
How long does dough keep in the fridge?
What do you do 1 hour before shaping?
choices: Take it out to warm up

drill.title: Scoop even cookies; space them on the pan
body: Cookies the same size bake in the same time. You'll scoop this week's cookie dough into even balls and space them so none bake together. Use this week's dough; this drill is part of baking it.
steps: Line a sheet pan with parchment.
Scoop a level tablespoon of dough. Scrape the top flat with a butter knife.
Roll it into a ball between your palms.
Make 12 balls. Line them up. Are they all the same? Pinch a bit from big ones onto small ones.
Place them on the pan in 4 rows of 3, about 2 inches apart.
Bake them as the recipe says. Did any touch? Were any darker than others?

quiz.q: Why make every cookie the same size?
choices: So they all bake in the same time
quiz.explain: Small ones burn while big ones are raw.

quiz.q: How far apart do the balls go?
How many fit on one pan?

knowledge.title: Why cookies spread
body: Some cookies come out thick and soft, and some come out thin and flat. A few things decide which.
Butter: soft butter beaten with sugar holds air and makes puffy cookies. Melted or very warm butter makes flat ones.
Flour: too little flour, and they spread. That's why you spoon and level. A warm pan spreads them too, so let the pan cool between batches.
Cold dough spreads less, because the butter takes longer to melt in the oven.
steps: Before you bake this week's cookies, put 2 balls of dough in the fridge for 30 minutes.
Bake 2 balls straight away, and the 2 cold ones beside them.
Which spread more? Draw them.
Answer out loud: name two things that make cookies spread.

quiz.q: What makes cookies spread flat?
choices: Melted butter or too little flour
quiz.explain: The butter melts before the cookie sets.

quiz.q: Which spreads less?
Why let the pan cool between batches?
choices: A hot pan makes the next cookies spread

sabbath.title: Freeze cookie dough balls
body: Cookie dough freezes well in balls. Freeze them once, and you can bake just 2 or 3 fresh cookies any time, right from the freezer.
steps: Scoop this week's dough into even balls. Set them on a parchment-lined pan or plate, close together but not touching.
Freeze them until hard, about 1 hour.
Move the frozen balls into a freezer bag. Write the name, the oven temperature, and the date on it.
They keep for 3 months.
To bake, don't thaw them. Set them 2 inches apart and bake 2 minutes longer than the recipe says.

quiz.q: Why freeze the balls on a pan first?
choices: So they don't stick together in the bag
quiz.explain: Then you take out only what you need.

quiz.q: Do you thaw frozen cookie dough before baking?
choices: No, bake it frozen, 2 minutes longer
quiz.explain: It bakes right from the freezer.

quiz.q: What goes on the bag?
choices: The name, oven temperature, and date
quiz.explain: So you know how to bake them.

drill.title: Toothpick test for doneness
body: The toothpick test tells you when the middle of a bake is done. You'll try it on this week's loaf before it's ready and again when it is, so you know what both look like.
steps: 10 minutes before the timer ends, have an adult pull out the rack.
Push a toothpick into the very center and pull it out. Look at it. Draw what you see.
Close the oven and keep baking.
When the timer ends, test again in the very center with a new toothpick. Draw it.
Clean, or a few moist crumbs, means done. Wet batter means 5 more minutes.
Compare your two drawings.

quiz.q: Where do you push the toothpick?
What does wet batter on the toothpick mean?
quiz.explain: Bake 5 more minutes and test again.

quiz.q: What does a done toothpick look like?
choices: Clean, or a few moist crumbs

knowledge.title: Quick breads around the world
body: Almost every country has a quick bread: a bread raised without yeast, mixed fast, and baked the same day.

Ireland has soda bread, raised with baking soda and buttermilk. The American South has cornbread, baked in a hot skillet. Banana bread came from American home kitchens. Mexico has pan de elote, a sweet corn cake. Brazil has pão de queijo, made with tapioca flour. Wales has Welsh cakes, cooked on a griddle.
They're all mixed the same way: dry things in one bowl, wet in another, then stirred together just until mixed.
steps: Find Ireland, the United States, Mexico, Brazil, and Wales on a map.
Write each quick bread next to its country.
Pick one you haven't made. Find out what it's served with.

quiz.q: What is a quick bread?
quiz.explain: Baking soda or powder raises it.

quiz.q: Which country is soda bread from?
quiz.explain: It's raised with baking soda and buttermilk.

quiz.q: What flour is in pão de queijo?
quiz.explain: It comes from the cassava root.

sabbath.title: Elijah and the widow's flour and oil (1 Kings 17:8–16)
body: Elijah was a prophet in a time with no rain, and food had run out. God sent him to a widow in a town called Zarephath (1 Kings 17:8–9).

She had only a handful of flour and a little oil, just enough for one last small loaf for herself and her son. Elijah asked her to make a little cake for him first, and told her God's promise: the flour and oil would not run out until the rain came (1 Kings 17:12–14).
She did what he said. "The jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil become empty" (1 Kings 17:16). There was food for many days.
steps: Read 1 Kings 17:8–16 with an adult.
What did the widow have left? Measure out a handful of flour and look at how little it is.
What did Elijah ask her to do first?
Answer out loud: how did the widow show she trusted God?
Share a slice of this week's bread with someone.

quiz.q: What did the widow have left?
choices: A handful of flour and a little oil

quiz.q: What did God promise?
choices: The flour and oil wouldn't run out

quiz.q: Who did the widow make the first cake for?

drill.title: Set up a steamer basket; steam broccoli
body: A steamer basket holds food above boiling water so the steam can cook it. You'll set one up and steam broccoli until it's bright green and just tender. Use the broccoli this week's potstickers already buy; for the gyeran-jjim week, buy one small head. An adult is at the stove with you.
steps: Put the steamer basket in a pot. Pour in water until it's just below the basket.
Put the lid on and bring the water to a boil over high heat.
Cut the broccoli into pieces about the same size.
With oven mitts, lift the lid far side first. Add the broccoli. Put the lid back on.
After 3 minutes, lift the lid away from you. Take out one piece with tongs.
Take out another piece at 4, 5, and 6 minutes. Line them up in order.
Taste each one after it cools. Which was best? Write down the minute.

quiz.q: Where does the water go?
quiz.explain: The food sits above the water.

quiz.q: What does perfect steamed broccoli look like?
choices: Bright green, with a little bite

quiz.q: Why line up the pieces in order?
choices: To see how cooking changes them

knowledge.title: Steam burns: lift a lid away from you
body: Steam is the hot cloud that rises from boiling water. It's as hot as the boiling water, about 212°F, and it can burn you just as badly.
Steam burns happen most when a lid comes off. The steam rushes out all at once, straight up into your face and over your hand.
So lift a lid by the far side first. The lid tips up like a shield between you and the steam. Wear oven mitts, keep your face back, and never reach across a steaming pot.
Microwave bowls and bags of steamed vegetables hold steam too. Open them on the side away from you.
steps: With an adult, practice with a cold pot: put on oven mitts and lift the lid far side first.
Say out loud where the steam would go.
Find two things in your kitchen that make steam.

quiz.q: When do most steam burns happen?
quiz.explain: The steam rushes out all at once.

quiz.q: Which side of the lid do you lift first?
How do you open a hot microwave bowl?
choices: On the side away from you

sabbath.title: Steam vegetables ahead for the week
body: Steamed vegetables keep well in the fridge for 3 to 4 days. Steam a big batch once, and you have a vegetable ready for several meals.
Stop the steaming a minute early. They'll soften a little more when you warm them up later.
Cool them fast: spread them on a plate, then put them in a container in the fridge within 2 hours.
steps: Steam a big batch of broccoli, carrots, or green beans, 1 minute less than you like them.
Spread them on a plate to cool for 10 minutes.
Pack them in a container. Label it with the date.
Later in the week, warm a serving in the microwave, covered, until hot.
Write down how many meals your batch helped with.

quiz.q: How long do steamed vegetables keep in the fridge?
Why steam them a minute less?
choices: They soften more when you warm them

quiz.q: How soon should they go in the fridge?

drill.title: Boil eggs soft and hard; ice bath and peel
body: You'll boil eggs two ways, soft and hard, and see how time changes them. Use 2 of the eggs this week's recipe already buys. An adult is at the stove with you.
steps: Put 2 eggs in a small saucepan with the slotted spoon. Cover them with cold water by 1 inch.
Wash your hands with soap.
Bring the water to a boil. Turn off the burner and put the lid on.
At 6 minutes, lift out one egg into a bowl of ice water.
At 12 minutes, lift out the other egg into the ice water.
After 5 minutes, tap, roll, and peel both eggs from the wide end.
Cut each in half. Draw the two yolks. Which is soft? Which is hard?

quiz.q: What makes a soft-boiled egg?
choices: A shorter time in the hot water

quiz.q: Why move the eggs to ice water?
choices: To stop the cooking and help them peel

quiz.q: Where do you start peeling?

knowledge.title: Egg freshness and the float test
body: Eggs keep a long time in the fridge, about 3 to 5 weeks. But as they get older, they slowly dry out inside, and a pocket of air at the wide end grows bigger.
That air pocket gives you a test. Put an egg in a bowl of cold water. A very fresh egg lies flat on the bottom. An older egg tips up on its end. An egg that floats is very old; throw it away.
Fresh eggs are best for frying and poaching. Eggs that are a week or two old are best for hard-boiling, because they peel more easily.
Check the date on the carton, keep eggs in the fridge, and throw away any egg that's cracked or smells bad.
steps: Fill a bowl with cold water.
Gently lower in the eggs from this week, one at a time.

sabbath.title: Boil eggs ahead for the week
body: Hard-boiled eggs are a quick breakfast, snack, or salad topping. Boil a dozen at once, and they're ready all week.
Keep them in their shells in the fridge, and eat them within 7 days. Peeled eggs keep a little less well, so peel each one when you eat it.
Write the date on the carton or container, so no one forgets when they were cooked.

drill.title: Measure rice and water; keep the lid on
body: You'll cook a small pot of rice by the ratio and keep the lid on the whole time. Use the rice this week's recipe already buys. An adult is at the stove with you.
steps: Measure ½ cup of long-grain rice. Rinse it in a strainer or colander until the water is almost clear.
Measure ¾ cup of water. Put the rice, water, and a pinch of salt in a small saucepan.
Bring it to a boil over high heat.
Put the lid on and turn the heat to low. Set a timer for 18 minutes.
Don't lift the lid. When the timer rings, turn off the heat and wait 5 more minutes.
Fluff the rice with a fork. Is it fluffy, crunchy, or mushy? Write it down.
Eat it with a meal this week, or cool it and keep it in the fridge for up to 4 days.

When do you turn the heat down?
choices: When it boils, with the lid on

knowledge.title: Why rice needs a set ratio
body: Rice cooked on the stove drinks up all its water. Nothing is poured off. So the amount of water has to be just right: this is called a ratio.
For long-grain white rice, the ratio is 1½ cups of water for every 1 cup of rice. Too little water, and the rice is crunchy. Too much, and it's mushy.
Keep the lid on. The last bit of water turns to steam, and the steam finishes cooking the rice. Lifting the lid lets the steam escape.
Different rice needs a different ratio. Brown rice takes about 2 cups of water. Short-grain rice, for sushi, takes a little less than long-grain.
steps: Write the ratio: 1 cup of rice, 1½ cups of water.
Work it out: how much water for 2 cups of rice? For ½ cup?
Look at a bag or box of rice. Find its ratio on the package and write it down.

sabbath.title: Feeding the five thousand (John 6:1–13)
body: A great crowd followed Jesus to a hillside by the Sea of Galilee. They were hungry, and there was nowhere nearby to buy food (John 6:1–5).
Andrew said, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?" (John 6:9). There were about five thousand men there.
Jesus had the people sit down. He took the loaves, gave thanks, and gave them out, and the fish too, "as much as they wanted" (John 6:11). Everyone ate until they were full.
Then Jesus said, "Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost" (John 6:12). They filled twelve baskets with what was left.

Answer out loud: what did the boy have?
Answer out loud: what did Jesus do before He gave out the food?

drill.title: Bring a pot to a boil, then turn it down to a simmer
body: You'll bring a pot of water to a boil, then turn it down to a simmer and hold it there. Use a pot of plain water. An adult is at the stove with you.
steps: Fill a saucepan halfway with water. Put it over high heat.
Watch it. Write down when you see tiny bubbles on the bottom.
Write down when big bubbles roll all over. That's a boil.
Turn the heat down to medium-low. Watch the bubbles get smaller.
Find the setting where small bubbles just break the top. That's a simmer.
Hold the simmer for 5 minutes. If it starts to boil, turn it down a little.
Turn off the stove. Write down which setting made a simmer on your stove.

quiz.q: What do you do if a simmer starts to boil?
choices: Turn the heat down a little

quiz.q: Which comes first when you heat water?
Why write down your simmer setting?

knowledge.title: Boil vs. simmer: what the bubbles mean
body: Bubbles tell you how hot a pot is. At a boil, big bubbles roll up all over the pot, fast and noisy. Water boils at 212°F.
At a simmer, small bubbles rise gently and just break the top. It's a little cooler than a boil.
Most soups and sauces cook at a simmer. A hard boil splashes, sticks to the bottom, breaks up soft food, and makes soup cloudy.
Cooks often bring a pot to a boil first, because it's fast, then turn it down to a simmer to cook.
steps: Look at this week's soup at a boil. Describe the bubbles.
Turn it down to a simmer. Describe the bubbles now.
Draw both pots: one boiling, one simmering.

quiz.q: What does a boil look like?
What does a simmer look like?
choices: Small bubbles just breaking the top

quiz.q: Why cook soup at a simmer?

sabbath.title: Freeze soup in portions
body: Soup freezes very well. Make a big pot once, and freeze it in portions for easy meals later.
Cool it first. Put it in the fridge within 2 hours, in shallow containers so it cools fast.
Freeze it in containers the size of one meal, leaving an inch at the top. Soup grows when it freezes.
Leave out the toppings, like chips and avocado. Add fresh ones when you eat it.
steps: Make a double batch of this week's soup, or save what's left.
Cool it in shallow containers in the fridge.
Spoon it into freezer containers, leaving an inch at the top.
Label each with the soup's name and the date. It keeps 3 months.
To eat, thaw it in the fridge overnight, then heat it until it bubbles.

drill.title: Drain pasta into a colander in the sink, safely
body: Draining pasta means pouring a heavy pot of boiling water into a colander. It's the most dangerous part of making pasta, so you'll practice it with plain water first, then with this week's spaghetti. An adult is next to you the whole time.

knowledge.title: Pasta shapes and what they're for
body: Pasta comes in hundreds of shapes, and each shape holds sauce in its own way.
Long, thin pasta, like spaghetti, goes with smooth sauces that coat each strand: marinara, or cheese and pepper.
Tubes, like penne and rigatoni, catch chunky sauces inside. Twists, like rotini and fusilli, trap sauce in their spirals. Little shapes, like elbows and orzo, go in soups and salads.
Most pasta is made from wheat flour and water, so it has gluten. Gluten-free pasta is made from rice, corn, or beans, and cooks a little differently, so follow its box.
steps: Find all the pasta shapes in your kitchen or at the store.
For each one, write a sauce or soup that would go with it.
Pick your favorite shape and draw it.

Abraham promised a little and gave a feast, and he served his guests first. The guests were the LORD and two angels.
