drill.title: Mince parsley and onion fine; salt and drain tomatoes
body: A salad or salsa is only as good as its smallest pieces. Today you'll mince parsley and onion as fine as you can, then run a side-by-side test on diced tomatoes: half salted and drained, half left alone. An adult is nearby the whole time.
steps: Set the cutting board on a damp paper towel. Rinse a bunch of parsley and roll it in a towel until the leaves are completely dry.

Pull the leaves off the thick stems. Gather them into a tight pile and rock the chef's knife through them, tip on the board and your other hand flat on the spine. Gather and rock again until the bits are about the size of a grain of rice.
Halve and peel an onion, leaving the root on. Mince one half: strips ⅛ inch apart toward the root, then across at ⅛ inch.
Core 2 tomatoes and dice them into ¼-inch cubes. Split the dice into two equal piles.
Put one pile in a strainer over a bowl and toss it with ¼ teaspoon of salt. Put the other pile in a dry bowl with no salt. Set a timer for 15 minutes.
When the timer rings, pour the liquid from under the strainer into a measuring spoon. How much came out? Tilt the unsalted bowl: how much is there?
Taste a cube from each pile. Write down how they differ in taste and in texture.

Stir the drained tomatoes, the onion, and a spoonful of the parsley together with a squeeze of lime for a quick salsa, or use them in this week's tostadas or tabbouleh today. Store the rest of the parsley and onion in labeled containers in the fridge for up to 3 days.

quiz.q: Why must parsley be completely dry before you mince it?
choices: Wet leaves bruise into a dark paste
quiz.explain: Dry leaves cut into clean, bright bits.

quiz.q: Which pile of tomatoes gave off more liquid?
quiz.explain: Salt draws water out of the cut cells. This week's Knowledge page explains how.

knowledge.title: Why salt draws water from cut vegetables
body: Every plant is made of cells, and each cell is a tiny bag of water held in by a thin membrane and a stiffer wall. A crisp cucumber or a firm tomato is crisp because those cells are full and pressing against each other, like balloons packed in a box.

Water moves across a cell's membrane toward the side with more dissolved in it, salt or sugar, until the two sides are closer to even. This is called osmosis. When you sprinkle salt on a cut vegetable, the salt dissolves in the juice on the surface and makes it far saltier than the water inside the cells. Water moves out of the cells toward the salt.

Cutting speeds it up. A whole tomato has a skin that salt can't get through; a diced tomato has hundreds of cut faces with opened cells. The smaller the dice, the more cut surface, and the faster the water comes out. That's why salted, diced tomatoes can give up a tablespoon or more of juice in 15 minutes.

Cooks use this on purpose. Tomatoes are salted and drained for pico de gallo so the salsa isn't soupy. Cucumbers are salted and squeezed before they go into a yogurt sauce so it stays thick. Eggplant was salted in Unit 1's ajapsandali so it would brown instead of steam. Shredded cabbage is salted for slaw so it softens and doesn't water down the dressing.

It also works against you. Salt a green salad and walk away, and twenty minutes later the leaves are limp and there's a puddle in the bowl. So the rule has two halves: salt early when you want water out, and salt at the last minute when you want things crisp.

Salt drawn into the drained vegetable stays in it, so a salted tomato is already seasoned. Taste before you add more. And not all salt measures alike: a teaspoon of fine table salt is about twice as salty as a teaspoon of flaky kosher salt, because the fine grains pack tighter in the spoon. The app's recipes use table salt unless they say otherwise.
steps: Slice a cucumber into thin rounds and split them into two plates.
Sprinkle one plate with ¼ teaspoon of salt. Leave the other plain.
After 20 minutes, look at each plate and try bending a slice from each. Write down what you see and feel.
Pat the salted slices dry and taste one from each plate. Which would you rather have in a yogurt dip, and which in a green salad? Why?

quiz.q: What is osmosis?
choices: Water moving toward the side with more dissolved in it
quiz.explain: Water moves out of the cells toward the salty surface.

quiz.q: Why does a diced tomato give up water faster than a whole one?
choices: It has more cut surface with opened cells
quiz.explain: The skin blocks salt; cut faces let water out.

quiz.q: When should you salt a green salad?
quiz.explain: Salt pulls water out of the leaves and wilts them.

quiz.q: Why are cucumbers salted before they go into a yogurt sauce?
choices: So their water comes out before, not in the sauce
quiz.explain: Squeezed cucumbers keep the sauce thick.

quiz.q: Which is saltier: a teaspoon of fine table salt or a teaspoon of flaky kosher salt?
quiz.explain: Fine grains pack tighter in the spoon.

sabbath.title: Make dips and salsas ahead and store them
body: Most dips and salsas are made from raw or already-cooked ingredients, so they can be made a day or more before you need them. Some even taste better the next day, once the garlic, lemon, and spices have had time to spread through.

How long each one keeps in a sealed container in the fridge: bean dips and hummus, 4 to 5 days; yogurt dips like tzatziki, 3 to 4 days, if the cucumber was salted and squeezed first; cooked or blended salsas, 5 to 7 days; pico de gallo, 1 to 2 days, since the tomatoes keep weeping; guacamole, 1 day, with plastic wrap pressed right onto its surface so air can't brown it.

Three habits keep them safe and fresh. Make and store them in clean containers, and get them into the fridge within 2 hours of making. Label each one with what it is and the date. And serve from a clean spoon into a small bowl rather than dipping into the whole container, so crumbs and mouths stay out of what's left.
A dip made ahead leaves you with a snack ready to go, half a meal already done, and a dish you can bring when someone needs one.
steps: Make a quick bean dip: drain and rinse a can of white or pinto beans, then mash them with a fork with 2 tablespoons of olive oil, 1 tablespoon of lemon or lime juice, ¼ teaspoon of salt, and a pinch of cumin. Taste and adjust.
Make a second dip or salsa of your choice from this unit, such as a drained pico de gallo or a cucumber yogurt dip.
Pack each one in a clean, sealed container. Label it with the name and the date.
Taste each one on the day you make it, then again the next day and the day after. Write down how each one changed.
Serve them at a meal or as a snack, from a clean spoon into a small bowl.

quiz.q: Which keeps the shortest time in the fridge?
quiz.explain: About a day, with plastic pressed on its surface.

quiz.q: Why serve a dip from a clean spoon into a small bowl?
choices: To keep crumbs and mouths out of what's stored
quiz.explain: What goes back in the fridge stays clean.

quiz.q: How soon should a dip you made go into the fridge?
quiz.explain: After 2 hours in the danger zone, bacteria have had time to grow.

drill.title: Timed fine dice of a salad set, then whisk and balance its dressing
body: This is the unit's mastery drill: the cuts for a whole salad, timed, then a dressing you balance by taste alone. Write down your times and your dressing changes; you'll compare them with this week's recipe.
steps: Set out a cucumber, a red bell pepper, a red onion, and 2 tomatoes, washed. Set the board on a damp paper towel and start a timer.
Cut the cucumber into ¼-inch planks, sticks, and cubes.
Cut the sides off the pepper, trim the ribs, and dice it skin side down at ¼ inch.
Mince half the onion at ⅛ inch.
Core, seed, and dice the tomatoes at ¼ inch. Stop the timer and write down your time.
Line up 10 cubes of each vegetable against a ruler. How many of each are within ⅛ inch of ¼ inch?
In a small bowl, whisk 1 tablespoon of vinegar with a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon of mustard until the salt dissolves. Whisk in 3 tablespoons of oil in a thin stream.
Taste it on a cucumber cube. Change one thing at a time: a pinch of salt, a few drops of vinegar, or a teaspoon of oil. Taste again after each, and write down every change.
Toss the vegetables with the dressing and eat it today, or store the pepper and onion apart for this week's recipe and use the cucumber and tomato today.

quiz.q: Why change only one thing at a time when balancing a dressing?
choices: So you know which change helped
quiz.explain: Change two at once and you can't tell which one did it.

quiz.q: Why dissolve the salt in the vinegar before the oil goes in?
choices: Salt dissolves in vinegar but not in oil
quiz.explain: Salt in oil stays as grains.

knowledge.title: Emulsions and the 3-to-1 rule; why salads go soggy, and dressing at the last minute
body: An emulsion is one liquid spread through another as tiny drops, when the two would normally stay apart. Oil and vinegar are the classic pair: vinegar is mostly water, and oil and water don't mix. Whisk them hard and the oil breaks into drops small enough to cloud the vinegar. That's an emulsion, at least for a few minutes.

Left alone, the drops find each other, join into bigger ones, and float to the top. That's why a plain vinaigrette splits. An emulsifier slows that down. It's something with one end that holds onto water and one end that holds onto oil, so it coats each drop and keeps it apart from the others. Mustard is the vinaigrette cook's emulsifier; egg yolk is mayonnaise's, which is why mayonnaise stays thick for weeks. Honey and garlic paste help too, by thickening the vinegar so drops move more slowly.

Drop size matters as much as the emulsifier. Pour the oil in slowly while whisking and each bit breaks into small drops the mustard can coat. Dump it all in and you get big drops that split fast. A shaken jar works too, because the shaking does the same job.

The 3-to-1 rule, three parts oil to one part acid, comes from French cooking, and it's a good starting point for wine vinegar. But acids vary. Lemon and lime juice are about as sharp as wine vinegar; rice vinegar is milder and can go closer to 2 to 1; balsamic is sweet and takes less oil. A dish matters too: mild ingredients like corn and beans can take a sharper dressing, as in this week's solterito. Start at 3 to 1, then taste.
Taste it on what it's going on. A dressing tasted from a spoon seems much stronger than it does on a leaf of lettuce. Dip a leaf or a cube of cucumber and judge it there.

Why salads go soggy: last week you saw salt pull water out of cut vegetables, and vinegar does the same. Oil is the other half. Lettuce leaves have a thin, waxy coat; oil soaks through it and darkens and wilts the leaf. Water left on the leaves from washing thins the dressing and keeps it from clinging. So: dry the leaves well, keep the dressing apart until the last minute, toss in a bowl bigger than you think you need, and start with less dressing than you think. You can always add more.

Not every salad needs the last-minute rule. A salad of sturdy chopped vegetables, beans, or grains, like tabbouleh or solterito, can sit dressed for an hour or two and gets better as the vegetables take on the dressing. Lettuce, tender herbs, and crisp croutons are the ones that can't wait.

quiz.q: What is an emulsion?
choices: One liquid spread through another as tiny drops
A mix of salt and water

quiz.q: What does mustard do in a vinaigrette?
choices: Coats the oil drops so they stay apart longer

quiz.q: Why pour the oil in slowly while whisking?
choices: It breaks into smaller drops that stay mixed

quiz.q: Where should you taste a dressing?
choices: On a leaf or piece of what it's dressing
quiz.explain: It tastes much stronger from a spoon.

quiz.q: Which salad can be dressed an hour ahead?
quiz.explain: Sturdy vegetables and beans get better as they sit.

sabbath.title: Salt (Leviticus 2:13; Matthew 5:13; Colossians 4:6)
body: In the ancient world, salt was precious. It seasoned food, and long before refrigerators, it kept meat and fish from spoiling. Israel got its salt from the Dead Sea, which the Bible calls the Salt Sea (Genesis 14:3).

God told Israel: "You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt" (Leviticus 2:13). Salt doesn't spoil, so a "covenant of salt" pictured a promise that lasts (Numbers 18:19).

Jesus told His followers, "You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet" (Matthew 5:13). Salt is meant to make a difference to everything it touches, and so are they.

Paul wrote, "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person" (Colossians 4:6). Like well-seasoned food, good words aren't bland, and they aren't too much.

In the kitchen, salt does more than taste salty. It brings out the other flavors in a dish, pulls water out of vegetables (that's how it helps them sweat), and keeps food from spoiling. Good cooks salt in stages, a little in each part of a dish, and taste before serving, the way you did this week.
steps: Read Leviticus 2:13 and Numbers 18:19.
Read Matthew 5:13–16.
Read Colossians 4:5–6.
Answer in writing: name two things salt does in food. How does each one fit what Jesus said about His followers?
Answer in writing: what would speech "seasoned with salt" sound like? Give an example from your week.
At a meal this week, taste a dish before and after a small pinch of salt, and talk with your family about what changed.

quiz.q: In Leviticus 2:13, what was to go with every grain offering?
quiz.explain: Leviticus 2:11 kept leaven and honey out of the offerings by fire.

quiz.q: Who did Jesus call "the salt of the earth"?
In Colossians 4:6, what should be "seasoned with salt"?

drill.title: Calibrate a thermometer in ice water
body: Every safe-temperature check this year depends on your thermometer reading correctly. A mixture of ice and water sits at 32°F, which makes it a reliable reference point.
steps: Fill a tall glass with ice, add cold water to just below the top of the ice, and stir. Let it stand 3 minutes.
Insert the probe at least 2 inches into the center of the glass, clear of the sides and bottom.
Wait for the reading to settle, about 30 seconds on a digital thermometer. It should read 32°F.

If it's more than 2°F off, recalibrate: most digital thermometers have a calibrate or reset function (see the manual); on a dial thermometer, an adult turns the nut under the dial with pliers until the needle reads 32°F. If it can't be adjusted, note the offset and correct for it every time.
Record readings for warm and cold tap water as well, so you get used to how quickly the probe settles.
Wash the probe in hot, soapy water. From now on, clean it after every use.

quiz.q: What should a calibrated thermometer read in ice water?
quiz.explain: An ice-water mixture stays at the freezing point of water, 32°F.

quiz.q: Why keep the probe away from the sides of the glass?
choices: The glass isn't the same temperature as the water
quiz.explain: You're measuring the water. The glass is warmer, so touching it skews the reading.

quiz.q: Your thermometer reads 35°F in ice water and can't be adjusted. A burger reads 162°F. What is it really?
quiz.explain: It reads 3°F high, so subtract 3. The burger needs another minute.

knowledge.title: The safe temperatures, and why ground meat differs from a whole cut
body: The USDA publishes a minimum safe internal temperature for each kind of food, measured in the thickest part.

Poultry, whole or ground: 165°F. Ground beef and ground lamb: 160°F. Egg dishes: 160°F. Fish: 145°F. Leftovers and reheated food: 165°F. Whole cuts of beef and lamb (steaks, chops, roasts): 145°F with a 3-minute rest, which is medium.

Plenty of people eat steak rare (about 125°F) or medium-rare (about 135°F). For an intact whole cut, that's a much smaller risk than undercooking ground meat. Pathogens sit on the surface of a whole muscle, and a hard sear kills them, while the interior is close to sterile. Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the whole batch, which is why ground meat has to reach 160°F all the way through.

That reasoning only holds for intact cuts. It doesn't cover ground meat, poultry, or meat that has been needle-tenderized or injected with a marinade (the label will say so), and it doesn't cover anyone at higher risk: pregnant women, young children, older adults, or anyone with a weakened immune system.
For an accurate reading, put the tip in the thickest part, away from bone and the pan. With thin pieces, go in from the side, and check more than one piece.
steps: Make a temperature card: poultry 165°F, ground beef and lamb 160°F, eggs 160°F, fish 145°F, whole cuts 145°F (USDA), reheating 165°F.
Post it inside a cupboard door by the stove.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground turkey need to reach?
quiz.explain: All poultry, ground or whole, is 165°F.

quiz.q: Why is a rare steak lower risk than a rare burger?
choices: Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the meat; a steak's interior is nearly sterile
quiz.explain: Searing kills what's on a steak's surface. A burger's surface bacteria are mixed all the way through.

quiz.q: Which of these should never be served rare?
quiz.explain: Tenderizing pushes surface bacteria into the middle, so it needs the same care as ground meat.

sabbath.title: Clean land animals you might not expect (Leviticus 11:1–8; Deuteronomy 14:3–8)
body: In Leviticus 11, God gave Israel two tests for land animals: "Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat" (Leviticus 11:3). An animal has to pass both. Its hoof is split into two toes, and it chews the cud, bringing swallowed food back up to chew again, the way a cow does.

The next verses name four animals that pass only one test. The camel, the rock badger, and the hare chew the cud but don't have a split hoof. The pig has a split hoof but doesn't chew the cud (Leviticus 11:4–7). Passing one test isn't enough.

Deuteronomy names the animals Israel may eat: "the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep" (Deuteronomy 14:4–5). Seven of the ten are wild animals.

The same two tests work for animals Israel never saw. Elk, moose, and caribou (called reindeer in Europe) are deer: split hooves, and they chew the cud. Water buffalo, yak, and bison are relatives of cattle, and the pronghorn of the American plains passes both tests too. All of them are clean. Bison and elk are sold in many grocery stores today, often ground, and can stand in for ground beef in this week's burgers. They're leaner, so cook them gently, and still to 160°F.
steps: Read Leviticus 11:1–8.
Read Deuteronomy 14:3–8.
Make a chart with two columns, "Split hoof" and "Chews the cud". Put each animal named in both passages under every test it passes.
Answer in writing: why isn't passing one test enough? Which animals in Leviticus 11:4–7 pass only one?
Research the giraffe. Does it have split hooves? Does it chew the cud? Based on this, is it clean to eat?
With an adult, look for bison or elk at a grocery store or butcher, and write down what you find.

quiz.q: What two tests does Leviticus 11:3 give for land animals?
choices: A split hoof and chewing the cud
Eating grass and living on land
quiz.explain: An animal has to pass both.

quiz.q: Why is the camel unclean?
choices: It chews the cud but doesn't have a split hoof
It has a split hoof but doesn't chew the cud

quiz.q: Which of these is clean?
quiz.explain: Elk are deer: split hooves, and they chew the cud.

weeks.title: Baked fish with lemon and herbs

drill.title: Check a fillet for pin bones; judge freshness by smell, eyes, and flesh
body: Many fish have a row of thin, soft pin bones that the filleting knife misses. You'll learn to find them by feel and pull them out, using the fish you bought for this week's recipe.
Fresh fish tells you it's fresh with its smell, its eyes, and its flesh. Take the second half of this drill to the fish counter when you buy this week's fish.
steps: Use the fillets for this week's recipe: salmon for the baked fish, or cod for the chermoula. Don't buy extra fish for the drill.

Lay a fillet skin side down, or flat side down if it's skinless. Run your fingertips slowly along the middle of the thick end, from the head end toward the tail, then back the other way. Feel for little hard tips poking up.
Press the flesh down gently on either side of a bone so it stands up. Grip its tip with clean tweezers and pull it out toward the head end, at the same angle it lies, so the flesh doesn't tear.
Line up the bones you pulled on a paper towel and count them. Check the fillet once more.

Check every fillet the same way. Write down how many bones you found and where. To see how a salmon and a white fish differ, watch a short video of a fishmonger pin-boning each (search "how to remove pin bones from salmon").
Wash your hands, the tweezers, and everything the raw fish touched. Wrap the fillets and keep them in the coldest part of the fridge for this week's recipe.
At the counter, look at a whole fish if there is one. Fresh eyes are clear and bulge a little; old ones are cloudy and sunken. Fresh gills are bright red, not brown.
Look at the fillets. Fresh flesh is moist and shiny, with no dry or browning edges, and the flakes hold together without gaps.
Ask to smell the fish you're buying. Fresh fish smells clean, like cold water or the sea. A strong fishy or sour smell means it's old.
At home, press the fillet gently with a fingertip. Fresh flesh springs back; old flesh keeps the dent.
Write down what you saw, smelled, and felt for each fish you checked.
Keep the fish in the coldest part of the fridge, on a plate on the bottom shelf, and cook it within a day.

quiz.q: Which way do you pull a pin bone?
choices: Toward the head end, at the angle it lies
Straight up as hard as you can
quiz.explain: Pulled the right way, the flesh doesn't tear.

quiz.q: How long can raw fish wait in the fridge?
quiz.explain: Cook it within a day or freeze it.

quiz.q: How do fresh fish eyes look?
quiz.explain: Cloudy, sunken eyes mean an old fish.

quiz.q: What should fresh fish smell like?
choices: Clean, like cold water or the sea
quiz.explain: A strong fishy smell means it's old.

knowledge.title: Fins and scales: clean and unclean species; reading fish labels and names
body: For animals that live in water, God gave Israel one test with two parts: "Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat" (Leviticus 11:9). Anything in the water without both is unclean (Leviticus 11:10–12; Deuteronomy 14:9–10).

Fins are easy to see. Scales are the thin, overlapping plates that cover most fish like roof tiles. Some fish have scales so small you have to look closely, like tuna and mackerel, but they're there, and the fish is clean.

Clean fish this app uses include salmon, trout, cod, tilapia, pollock, haddock, halibut, tuna, sardines, anchovies, and many more: carp, herring, mackerel, smelt, whitefish, perch, walleye, pike, bass, barramundi, mahi-mahi, snapper, grouper, sole, and flounder.

What the test leaves out: every animal with a shell, the soft sea animals with arms and no backbone, and fish with smooth, slippery skin and no scales, such as the whiskered bottom-feeders sold as swai or basa, and monkfish. Swordfish and sturgeon lose most of their scales as they grow, and people disagree about them, so this app leaves them out.
Once a fish is filleted and its skin is off, you can't see the scales anymore. That's why the name on the label matters, which the second half of this page covers.

A fillet with its skin off can't show you its scales, so the label has to. In the United States, fish labels must name the fish and say where it came from and whether it was wild-caught or farm-raised. Read the name first, every time.

Some names are general. "Whitefish" can mean a real whitefish, or it can be a catch-all for any white-fleshed fish. "Sea bass" and "rockfish" cover several kinds. When a label is vague, ask at the counter which fish it is, and pass on it if no one knows.
Some cheap white fillets come from smooth-skinned river fish with no scales, sold as swai or basa. They look just like cod or tilapia, so read the label.

Prepared fish hides even more. Fish sticks and frozen fish fillets are usually pollock or cod, and the box says so. Imitation seafood sticks, called surimi, are often pollock but can include extracts from animals that aren't clean, so skip them unless the full ingredient list is clean.
Frozen fish is often fresher than "fresh": it's frozen on the boat or soon after. Fish labeled "previously frozen" at the counter should be cooked within a day and not frozen again.

quiz.q: What two things must a water animal have to be clean?
Tuna's scales are so small they're hard to see. Is tuna clean?
choices: Yes, it has fins and scales
No, the scales are too small

quiz.q: A fish has fins but smooth skin with no scales. Is it clean?
choices: Only if it lives in a river

quiz.q: Why does this app leave out swordfish?
choices: It loses most of its scales as it grows, so people disagree
quiz.explain: When in doubt, it's left out.

quiz.q: Which of these is clean?
quiz.explain: Swai and monkfish have smooth skin and no scales.

quiz.q: What's the first thing to read on a fish label?
quiz.explain: Without the skin, you can't see the scales.

quiz.q: A label says only "whitefish". What do you do?
choices: Ask which fish it is, and pass if no one knows
Buy it; all white fish are clean
quiz.explain: It can be a catch-all name.

quiz.q: Why read the full ingredient list on imitation seafood sticks?
choices: They can include extracts from animals that aren't clean
quiz.explain: They're often pollock, but not always only pollock.

quiz.q: Why can frozen fish be fresher than fish at the counter?
choices: It's often frozen on the boat, right after it's caught
quiz.explain: "Fresh" fish may have traveled for days.

sabbath.title: Loaves and fishes, and breakfast on the shore (Matthew 14:13–21; John 21:9–13)
body: Fish was everyday food around the Sea of Galilee, where several of Jesus' disciples were fishermen. Twice the Gospels show Jesus feeding people bread and fish.

Once, a crowd followed Him into a remote place. When evening came, the disciples had only five loaves and two fish. Jesus looked up to heaven, blessed the food, broke the loaves, and gave them to the disciples to hand out. "And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over" (Matthew 14:20). About five thousand men ate, besides women and children.

After His resurrection, Jesus met seven of His disciples at the lake after a night of catching nothing. He told them where to cast the net, and they hauled in 153 large fish (John 21:11). On the shore "they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread" (John 21:9). "Jesus said to them, 'Come and have breakfast'" (John 21:12), and He served them the bread and the fish Himself.
Both meals were simple: bread and fish. In one, Jesus fed thousands from almost nothing; in the other, He cooked for a few tired friends.
steps: Read Matthew 14:13–21.
Read John 21:1–14.
Answer in writing: what did Jesus do with the food before it was handed out in Matthew 14:19?
Answer in writing: in John 21, who cooked breakfast, and what does that show you about Him?
Cook a simple meal of bread and fish for your family this week, from this week's recipe, and serve it to them yourself.

quiz.q: How many loaves and fish did the disciples have?
How many baskets of leftovers were taken up?
What did Jesus say to the disciples on the shore in John 21?

drill.title: Trim and cube chicken thighs; clean down after
body: Boneless thighs are the most forgiving cut of chicken, but they come with soft white fat, a few tough strands of gristle, and an uneven shape. Today you'll trim them clean and cut them into even 1-inch cubes, then clean down as if you'd been cooking in a restaurant kitchen. An adult is nearby the whole time.
Use the chicken for this week's recipe, or freeze the cubes flat in a labeled bag to cook within 3 months.
steps: Clear the counter and set out your raw-meat board on a damp paper towel, a sharp chef's knife, a bowl for the trimmed cubes, and a second bowl for scraps. Have hot, soapy water ready in the sink.
Open the package over the board so no juice drips on the counter. Don't rinse the chicken. Put the empty tray straight in the trash.

Unroll one thigh, smooth side down. Find the thick, soft white fat at the edges and in the folds. Pull it gently away with your fingers and cut it off with the tip of the knife, keeping the blade angled away from your other hand.
Feel for gristle: shiny, white, rubbery strands that don't give when you press them. Cut them out.
Cut the thigh into 1-inch strips, then across into 1-inch cubes. The thin edges make smaller pieces; put two small ones together in your count, or set them aside for a stir-fry.
Trim and cube the rest. Line up 10 cubes and look at them side by side: are they close to the same size?
Weigh the trimmings or measure them in a measuring cup. Write down how much of the package you trimmed away.

Clean down: scraps in the trash, the cubes covered in the fridge, then the knife, the board, and the bowls in hot, soapy water. Wipe the counter, the faucet handle, and anything else you touched with hot, soapy water. Wash your hands last, for at least 20 seconds.

quiz.q: What do you do before cutting raw chicken?
choices: Set up the raw-meat board and leave the chicken unrinsed
Rinse the chicken in the sink
Cut the vegetables on the same board right after
quiz.explain: Rinsing spreads bacteria. The board is set up first.

quiz.q: How do you know a strand is gristle, not meat?
choices: It's shiny, white, and rubbery, and doesn't give when pressed
quiz.explain: Soft white is fat; shiny and rubbery is gristle.

quiz.q: Why cut the cubes all close to 1 inch?
choices: So they all reach 165°F at the same time
quiz.explain: Big pieces finish last, and small ones dry out waiting.

quiz.q: What gets washed after cutting raw chicken?
choices: The knife, board, bowls, counter, faucet handle, and your hands
quiz.explain: Anything you touched with chicken on your hands, including the faucet.

knowledge.title: Cross-contamination and board colors; never rinse raw poultry
body: Cross-contamination is the transfer of microorganisms from one food or surface to another, usually from raw meat to something that won't be cooked, by way of hands, knives, boards, or towels.

Commercial kitchens color-code cutting boards: red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, blue for raw fish, green for produce. At home, two boards cover it: one only for raw meat, poultry, and fish, and one for everything else.
With a single board, work from clean to raw: ready-to-eat foods and produce first, raw meat last, then wash the board, knife, and your hands in hot, soapy water.

Don't rinse raw poultry; it sprays bacteria around the sink and doesn't remove them. Cooked food goes on a clean plate, never the one that held it raw. Wash your hands after handling raw meat, eggs, or their packaging.
steps: Choose one cutting board for raw meat, poultry, and fish only, and mark it.
Go through this week's recipe and list every step that involves raw chicken or raw egg: what it touches, and where that gets washed.

quiz.q: With one cutting board, what order do you work in?
quiz.explain: Anything cut after raw meat on the same board picks up its bacteria.

quiz.q: Should you rinse raw chicken?
choices: No, it spreads bacteria without removing them
quiz.explain: Cooking to 165°F is what makes chicken safe.

quiz.q: The chicken is cooked. Where does it go?
choices: The plate it sat on raw
quiz.explain: Anything that held raw meat still carries its bacteria.

sabbath.title: Clean and unclean birds, and why God gave the food laws (Leviticus 11:13–19, 44–47)
body: For land animals and fish, Leviticus gives a test. For birds it gives a list instead: "And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten" (Leviticus 11:13). Twenty kinds follow, among them the eagle, the vultures, the kite and falcon, every raven, the ostrich, the hawk, the owls, the cormorant, the stork, the heron, and the bat, which the passage counts with the birds (Leviticus 11:13–19; Deuteronomy 14:11–18).

Most of the birds on the list hunt other animals or eat what's already dead. Every bird not on it may be eaten: "You may eat all clean birds" (Deuteronomy 14:11). Scripture also shows clean birds in use. Pigeons and turtledoves were brought as offerings (Leviticus 1:14; 12:8), and God fed Israel quail in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13; Numbers 11:31). Chicken, turkey, duck, goose, quail, pigeon and dove, pheasant, partridge, grouse, and guinea fowl are all clean, and this app uses them.

Leviticus 11 also says why the food laws were given. "For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44). The chapter ends: "This is the law about beast and bird and every living creature that moves through the waters and every creature that swarms on the ground, to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten" (Leviticus 11:46–47).
The reason the passage itself gives is about God: His people were to be set apart, holy, because He is holy. Choosing food carefully was one everyday way to live that out, at every meal.
steps: Read Leviticus 11:13–19 and 11:44–47.
Read Deuteronomy 14:11–20.
List every bird named in Leviticus 11:13–19. Next to each, write whether it hunts, eats dead animals, or something else, using a field guide or a reliable website.
Find two places in Scripture where clean birds are offered or eaten (start with Leviticus 1:14 and Exodus 16:13), and write down what happened.
Answer in writing: what reason does Leviticus 11:44–45 give for the food laws? Put it in your own words.
Look at the poultry case at a grocery store with an adult. Write down every kind of bird you find, and check each against the list.

quiz.q: How does Leviticus 11 tell clean birds from unclean?
choices: It lists the unclean birds by name
It says all birds are clean
quiz.explain: Land animals and fish get a test; birds get a list.

quiz.q: Which of these is clean?
quiz.explain: God fed Israel quail in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13).

quiz.q: What reason does Leviticus 11:44 give for the food laws?
quiz.explain: The passage ties the laws to God's holiness.

quiz.q: What do most of the unclean birds have in common?
choices: They hunt other animals or eat dead ones
quiz.explain: Eagles, hawks, and owls hunt; vultures and ravens eat what's dead.

drill.title: Thaw safely and set up a raw-meat station unaided
body: Set up your own clean station without help. An adult checks it against the list but doesn't step in.
steps: Clear the counter of anything you won't use. Wash it with hot, soapy water and dry it.
Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.
Set out both cutting boards, raw-meat and general, each on a damp paper towel.
Set out a plate for raw meat, a separate plate for cooked food, and a bowl for scraps.
Calibrate the thermometer in ice water (week 7) and keep it within reach.
Fill one side of the sink or a dishpan with hot, soapy water for washing as you go.
Have the adult check your setup against this list, then cook this week's recipe from it.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands?
quiz.explain: That's the CDC guideline, with soap, scrubbing every surface.

quiz.q: Why two plates?
choices: One for raw meat, one for cooked food
quiz.explain: Cooked food never goes back on the raw plate.

knowledge.title: Cuts: dark vs. white, tender vs. tough, fillet types; carryover (unit quiz)
body: Knowing the cut tells you how to cook it. This page covers the cuts this unit used and the ones you'll meet next, then one more idea about temperature, and ends with a quiz on the whole unit.

Dark and white meat. Chicken legs and thighs do the walking, so their muscles have more fat, more connective tissue, and more of the red protein that stores oxygen. That makes them darker, richer, and hard to dry out: thighs stay juicy even a few degrees past 165°F. Breasts barely work, so they're lean, mild, and pale, and they turn dry fast once they pass 165°F. That's why breasts are cut even and watched closely, as in this week's tenders.

Tender and tough. On a cow or a lamb, the muscles that work hardest (shoulder, leg, shank, brisket) are full of connective tissue, which is chewy when cooked fast. Long, slow, moist heat melts it into gelatin, so those cuts are braised or stewed. The muscles along the back that do little work (ribeye, sirloin, tenderloin, lamb loin chops) are tender and are cooked fast and hot: seared, grilled, or broiled. Ground meat can go either way.

Fish fillets. Fish are sold as fillets (the side, cut off the bone), steaks (a slice across the body, with a bone in the middle), or whole. Lean, white, flaky fish like cod, tilapia, and haddock are delicate and suit baking, steaming, and gentle pan-frying. Oily fish like salmon, trout, and mackerel are richer, stay moist, and stand up to roasting and broiling. Firm, meaty fish like tuna and mahi-mahi hold together on a grill.

Carryover cooking. Food keeps cooking after it comes off the heat, because the outside is hotter than the middle and that heat keeps moving inward. A thick piece can rise 5°F or more as it rests; a thin strip, barely at all. Restaurant cooks use this, pulling a thick roast a few degrees early. This app always asks you to reach the safe temperature before the food comes off the heat, so the rest is a bonus, not part of the safety check. You'll use carryover on purpose with the big roasts later in the year.
steps: Make a two-column chart, "Cook fast and hot" and "Cook low and slow". Put each of these cuts in a column: chicken breast, chicken thigh, beef chuck, beef sirloin, lamb shank, lamb loin chop, flank steak, brisket.
Next time you cook something thick (a burger, a fillet, a kofta), check its temperature as it comes off the heat, then again after 3 minutes. Write down how much it rose.
Take the unit quiz below.

quiz.q: Why do thighs stay juicier than breasts?
choices: They have more fat and connective tissue
They cook at a lower temperature
quiz.explain: Hard-working muscles are richer and more forgiving.

quiz.q: Which cut would you braise slowly?
quiz.explain: Shoulder cuts are tough until slow, moist heat melts their connective tissue.

quiz.q: What is carryover cooking?
choices: Food rising in temperature after it leaves the heat
quiz.explain: Heat keeps moving from the hot outside into the middle.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground lamb need?
quiz.explain: Ground beef and lamb are 160°F; poultry is 165°F.

quiz.q: Your thermometer reads 34°F in ice water. A chicken strip reads 166°F. Is it done?
Which fish is clean?
Where do you feel for pin bones?
choices: Along the middle of the thick end of the fillet
quiz.explain: They sit in a line through the thickest part (week 8).

quiz.q: You have one cutting board. What order do you cut in?
choices: Vegetables first, raw chicken last, then wash
Any order if you rinse the board with water
quiz.explain: Clean to raw, then hot, soapy water (week 9).

quiz.q: Why don't you rinse raw chicken?
choices: It splashes bacteria around without removing them
quiz.explain: Cooking to 165°F is what makes it safe (week 9).

quiz.q: What may be done with marinade that held raw chicken?
choices: Brush it on the cooked chicken

quiz.q: Which bird is clean?
quiz.explain: Herons and owls are on the list in Leviticus 11:13–19 (week 9).

quiz.q: What are the two tests for land animals?
choices: A split hoof and chewing the cud
Eating grass and living on land

sabbath.title: Blood and fat (Leviticus 3:17; 7:23–27; 17:10–14)
body: Two more food laws run alongside the clean and unclean animals: no blood, and no fat of certain kinds. "It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood" (Leviticus 3:17).

Blood. The rule is older than Israel. After the flood, God told Noah, "But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood" (Genesis 9:4). Leviticus gives the reason: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls" (Leviticus 17:11). A hunter who killed a clean animal or bird was to "pour out its blood and cover it with earth" (Leviticus 17:13).

In the kitchen, the blood is drained at slaughter, before the meat reaches a store. The red liquid in a package of beef is mostly water and a protein called myoglobin, not blood. Some families who keep these laws buy only kosher or halal meat, which is drained and handled under its own rules; others buy ordinary meat. Either way, this app never uses blood as an ingredient, and no recipe uses dishes made from it, which some cuisines sell as sausages, puddings, or cakes.

Fat. "You shall eat no fat, of ox or sheep or goat" (Leviticus 7:23). In the offerings, "the fat" means the thick, hard fat around the organs and kidneys, which was burned on the altar (Leviticus 3:3–5). It doesn't mean the fat marbled through meat. This app follows that: the hard fat of cattle, sheep, and goats, and the cooking fat rendered from it, are never used. Marbling, and the juices and drippings from cooking, are fine. Watch for that hard fat in some pastry, mincemeat, dumplings, and in the oil some restaurants fry in.
So a clean animal, drained of its blood, without its hard fat: those three together are what this unit has meant by clean meat.
steps: Read Leviticus 3:17; 7:22–27; and 17:10–14.
Read Genesis 9:3–4.
Answer in writing: what reason does Leviticus 17:11 give for not eating blood?
Answer in writing: what's the difference between the fat Leviticus 3:3–5 describes and the marbling in a steak?
With an adult, read the labels on three store-bought items that could hide animal fat (pie crust, a box of mincemeat, or a frozen pastry). Write down which fats each one uses.

quiz.q: Where does the rule against eating blood first appear?
quiz.explain: God gave it to Noah, before Israel.

quiz.q: What reason does Leviticus 17:11 give?
choices: The life of the flesh is in the blood

quiz.q: Is the red liquid in a package of beef blood?
choices: Mostly no: it's water and a protein called myoglobin
quiz.explain: The blood is drained at slaughter.

quiz.q: Which fat does this app leave out?
choices: The hard fat of cattle, sheep, and goats around the organs, and fat rendered from it
quiz.explain: Marbling and pan juices are fine (Leviticus 3:3–5; 7:23).

drill.title: Spoon and level vs. weigh flour; the muffin method, stopped while streaky
body: Two habits make quick breads come out the same every time: measuring flour the same way, and mixing just enough. You'll measure one cup of flour three ways and weigh each, then mix two small batters to the same recipe, one stopped while streaky and one stirred smooth, and cook them side by side as pancakes.
Use the flour and buttermilk this week's bread already buys. An adult is nearby for the stove.
steps: Set a bowl on the kitchen scale and zero it. Scoop the measuring cup straight into the flour bag, level it with the back of a knife, and tip it into the bowl. Write down the weight.
Pour that flour back. Fluff the flour in the bag with a spoon, spoon it into the cup without packing, and level it. Weigh it and write it down.
Do the spoon-and-level cup two more times and weigh each. A cup of all-purpose flour should weigh about 4.4 ounces. How far off was the scooped cup?
In each of two small bowls, whisk together 3 tablespoons of flour, ½ teaspoon of sugar, ¼ teaspoon of baking powder, and a pinch of salt.
In a cup, whisk ⅓ cup of buttermilk with 2 teaspoons of oil. Pour half into each bowl.
Bowl A: fold with a spatula, about 8 strokes, and stop while a few streaks of flour still show. Bowl B: stir hard with a whisk for 1 minute, until it's completely smooth.
Heat a skillet over medium heat with a little oil. Spoon in each batter as one pancake, side by side, and cook until bubbles cover the top, then flip and cook 1 more minute.
Let them cool a minute, then tear each in half. Compare how tall they are, how tender they are, and what the inside looks like.
Write down what you found, and turn off the stove.

quiz.q: Why does a scooped cup of flour weigh more?
choices: The cup packs the flour down
quiz.explain: That can be a quarter more flour than the recipe means.

quiz.q: About how much does a cup of all-purpose flour weigh?
Which pancake is usually more tender?
quiz.explain: Stirring builds gluten, which makes it tough.

quiz.q: In the muffin method, what gets mixed separately?
choices: The dry ingredients and the wet ones
quiz.explain: Then they're folded together only until just combined.

knowledge.title: Baking soda vs. baking powder; doneness by toothpick and temperature
body: Quick breads rise without yeast. A chemical leavener makes carbon dioxide gas in the batter, and the oven sets the batter around the bubbles before they escape. There are two, and they aren't the same thing.

Baking soda is one ingredient, sodium bicarbonate. It makes gas only when it meets an acid: buttermilk, yogurt, lemon juice, brown sugar, honey, or natural cocoa. It starts working the moment the acid touches it, so a soda batter goes into the oven right away. Too much soda, or soda with too little acid, leaves a bitter, soapy taste and yellow-green specks.

Baking powder is baking soda with a dry acid already mixed in, plus a little starch to keep them apart. Most baking powder is double-acting: it makes some gas when it gets wet and more when it gets hot. It's used when the batter has no acid of its own, like plain milk. Many recipes use both: soda to match the buttermilk, and powder for extra lift.

A quick bread is done when its center is set. The toothpick test: push it into the center and pull it out. Wet batter means it needs more time; clean, or a few moist crumbs, means it's done. The thermometer is surer. Most quick breads are set at 200 to 205°F in the center, about 10°F hotter than a soft yeast bread, because there's more moisture to drive off.
Both leaveners lose strength with age. Write the date on the box when you open it. Old baking soda and powder still look the same, so test them.
steps: Test your baking soda: stir ¼ teaspoon into 2 tablespoons of vinegar in a glass. It should fizz hard at once.
Test your baking powder: stir ½ teaspoon into ¼ cup of hot tap water in a second glass. It should bubble right away.
Stir ¼ teaspoon of baking soda into ¼ cup of plain water in a third glass. Write down what happens and why.
Read the labels on your baking soda and baking powder. Write down what's in each.
Look at this week's recipe. Write down which leaveners it uses, and which ingredient is the acid for the baking soda.
When this week's bread comes out, do the toothpick test and the thermometer test on it, and write down what each told you.

quiz.q: What does baking soda need to make gas?
quiz.explain: In plain water, baking soda does almost nothing.

quiz.q: What is baking powder?
choices: Baking soda with a dry acid already mixed in
quiz.explain: It works in a batter that has no acid of its own.

quiz.q: Why does a buttermilk and soda batter go straight into the oven?
choices: The gas starts as soon as they meet, and escapes if it waits
quiz.explain: The oven has to set the batter around the bubbles.

quiz.q: What does a bitter, soapy taste in a quick bread mean?
choices: Too much baking soda, or not enough acid for it

quiz.q: About what temperature is a quick bread done at in the center?
quiz.explain: A little hotter than a soft yeast bread's 190°F.

sabbath.title: Bake and freeze quick breads
body: Quick breads are at their best warm on the day they're baked, and they go stale quickly on the counter. Frozen the right way, they come back almost fresh, so one baking day can cover several meals.

Staling is the starch in bread slowly hardening as it loses water. The fridge speeds it up; the freezer stops it. So quick breads are kept on the counter for a day or two, or frozen, but not refrigerated.
The bread has to be completely cool first. Warm bread wrapped up steams, and the crust turns soggy and ices over in the freezer.
steps: Let this week's cornbread or soda bread cool completely on a rack, at least 1 hour.
Cut it into the pieces you'll want to serve: wedges of cornbread, or slices of soda bread.
Wrap the pieces tightly in plastic wrap or foil, a meal's worth to a bundle, and put the bundles in a freezer bag. Press out the air.
Label the bag with the bread's name and the date. Quick breads keep in the freezer for up to 3 months.
To serve, take out what you need and let it thaw in its wrap on the counter, about 30 minutes for slices.
Unwrap it, lay it on a sheet pan, and warm it in a 350°F oven for 8 to 10 minutes, until the crust is crisp again.
Taste a warmed piece beside one kept on the counter for 2 days. Write down which is better and why.

quiz.q: Why are quick breads frozen instead of refrigerated?
choices: The fridge makes them stale faster; the freezer stops it
They can't go in the fridge
quiz.explain: Staling is fastest just above freezing.

quiz.q: Why does bread cool completely before wrapping?
choices: Warm bread steams in the wrap and turns soggy
quiz.explain: The steam freezes into ice on the crust.

quiz.q: How long do quick breads keep in the freezer?
quiz.explain: Label the bag with the date.

drill.title: Bloom yeast at 105–110°F; knead to a windowpane
body: You'll test yeast in water at three temperatures, side by side, and see for yourself why the recipe asks for 105 to 110°F. Use the thermometer you calibrated in week 7.
You'll knead a small dough by hand and test it as you go, so you learn what a developed dough feels like. There's no yeast in it; the drill is about gluten.
steps: Set out 3 clear glasses or jars and label them: cool, warm, hot.

Fill each with ½ cup of water: about 80°F in the first, 105 to 110°F in the second, and 140°F in the third. Warm the water in the microwave and check each glass with the thermometer, adjusting with hot or cold water until it reads right.
Stir ½ teaspoon of sugar into each glass.
Sprinkle ½ teaspoon of active dry yeast over each, and start a 10-minute timer.
At 5 minutes and at 10 minutes, look at each glass. Note how much foam there is and how it smells.
Write down what you saw: which bloomed fastest, which bloomed slowly, and which didn't bloom at all.
Pour the glasses down the drain and rinse them.
Stir together 1 cup of all-purpose flour, ⅓ cup of water, and a pinch of salt in a bowl until it forms a rough dough.
Turn it out and knead: push it away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it a quarter turn, and repeat in a steady rhythm.
After 2 minutes, pinch off a grape-sized piece and try the windowpane test: stretch it slowly between your fingers and thumbs into a thin sheet. Note where it tears.
Knead 3 more minutes and test again. Then 3 more, and test again.
Note how the dough changed: how sticky it is, how smooth, and how far it stretched each time.
When a piece stretches thin enough to see light through, the dough is developed. Note how many minutes it took.
Roll the dough thin and cook it in a dry skillet like Unleavened flatbread, or throw it out.

quiz.q: Which glass should show no foam?
The 80°F glass foamed, but slowly. Why?
choices: Cool water slows yeast but doesn't kill it
quiz.explain: Yeast still works when it's cool, just more slowly.

quiz.q: The test piece tore before it went thin. What next?
choices: Knead a few more minutes and test again

quiz.q: How does dough change as you knead it?

knowledge.title: How yeast makes dough rise; gluten and kneading
body: Baker's yeast is a single-celled fungus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. A packet holds billions of them, dried and dormant. Warm water wakes them up.

Once awake, yeast feeds on sugars in the dough, some added and some released from the flour's starch by its own enzymes. It breaks them down by fermentation and gives off two things: carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol (ethanol).

The gas is what raises bread. Kneading builds gluten, a stretchy network that traps the gas in thousands of tiny bubbles, so the dough swells instead of letting it escape. In the oven, the gas expands, the alcohol bakes off, and the heat kills the yeast at about 140°F. The bubbles set in place as the crumb.

Temperature runs the whole process. Yeast works best around 75 to 80°F in a rising dough. Cold slows it down; that's why a dough can rise overnight in the fridge. Water above about 130°F starts to kill it, which is why you check the water before the yeast goes in.
Fermentation also makes flavor. A dough that rises slowly, in a cool kitchen or the fridge, tastes fuller than one rushed in a warm spot.
Wheat flour holds two proteins, glutenin and gliadin. Dry, they do nothing. When water is added, they link up into gluten. Glutenin makes it springy and strong, and gliadin makes it stretchy.

Kneading lines those links up. At first the dough is shaggy and tears easily. As you push, fold, and turn it, the strands lengthen and organize into a network that stretches without breaking. That's what the windowpane test shows.
A strong network matters most for a tall loaf. It has to hold its gas through a long rise and half an hour in the oven. A flatbread, baked in minutes, needs less.

Other ingredients change gluten. Fat (butter, oil, egg yolk) coats the strands so the crumb is soft and tender; that's an enriched dough. Salt tightens the network and slows the yeast a little. Bread flour has more protein than all-purpose, so it builds stronger gluten and a chewier bread.

Gluten is also why some people can't eat bread. In people with celiac disease, gluten triggers an immune reaction that damages the small intestine. Gluten-free breads use other starches and binders, and they behave differently in every step you're learning.

quiz.q: What is baker's yeast?
quiz.explain: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a living fungus, dried and dormant in the packet.

quiz.q: Which gas raises bread dough?
quiz.explain: Yeast gives it off as it ferments sugar. Steam helps in the oven, as in pita.

quiz.q: What traps the gas in the dough?
quiz.explain: Gluten's stretchy network holds the gas in tiny bubbles.

quiz.q: What happens to yeast in the oven?
choices: It keeps working until the bread cools
quiz.explain: By then it has done its work, and the bubbles set as the crumb.

quiz.q: Why can dough rise overnight in the fridge?
choices: Cold slows yeast down without killing it
quiz.explain: That slow rise also gives the bread more flavor.

quiz.q: Which two proteins form gluten?
quiz.explain: Water lets them link; kneading lines them up.

quiz.q: What does kneading do?
choices: Lines up gluten strands into a strong network
quiz.explain: That network traps the yeast's gas.

quiz.q: Why is an enriched dough softer?
quiz.explain: Butter, oil, and egg yolk tenderize the crumb.

quiz.q: Why would a baker pick bread flour?
choices: Its higher protein builds stronger gluten
quiz.explain: Stronger gluten makes a taller, chewier loaf.

sabbath.title: Bread in the Bible: daily bread and the bread of life (Matthew 6:11; John 6:35)
body: Bread comes up more than almost any other food in the Bible. It stands for the food a person needs to live, and often for more than that.

In the wilderness, God fed Israel with manna, "bread from heaven" (Exodus 16:4). Each morning the people gathered what they needed for that day. Manna kept overnight spoiled, except the double portion gathered on the sixth day, which kept (Exodus 16:16–24). It taught them to depend on God one day at a time.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). The prayer asks for what's needed today, not a store for years.

After feeding five thousand people with five loaves (John 6:1–14), Jesus told the crowd, who had brought up the manna, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger" (John 6:35). Bread keeps a body alive for a day; He spoke of Himself as what keeps a person alive for good.
steps: Read Exodus 16:4–5 and 16:13–24.
Read Matthew 6:9–13.
Read John 6:26–35.
Answer in writing: what did gathering manna each morning teach Israel?
Answer in writing: why do you think Jesus compared Himself to bread, and not to some other food?
Share your answers with an adult at a meal this week, with a slice of this week's loaf.

quiz.q: What did Israel gather each morning in the wilderness?
Where is "Give us this day our daily bread"?
quiz.explain: It's part of the prayer Jesus taught in Matthew 6.

quiz.q: What happened just before Jesus said "I am the bread of life"?
choices: He fed five thousand people with five loaves
quiz.explain: The crowd followed Him after the feeding (John 6:1–14, 26).

drill.title: Shape even rolls by weight
body: Bakeries weigh dough because eyes are poor judges of size. You'll divide a practice dough by weight and shape tight, even balls.
steps: Stir together 1½ cups of all-purpose flour, ½ cup of water, and a pinch of salt until it forms a dough. Knead it until it's smooth, about 3 minutes.
Before using the scale, cut the dough by eye into 8 pieces you think are equal. Weigh each one and write the weights down.
Press the pieces back together. Weigh the whole dough and divide by 8. That's your target.
Cut 8 pieces again, this time weighing each. Pinch dough from heavy pieces onto light ones until each is within a tenth of an ounce of the target.
Shape each piece into a ball: cup it under your palm on a bare spot of counter and roll it in small circles until the top is smooth and tight.
Compare your two sets of weights. How far off were your eyes?
Roll the balls flat and cook them in a dry skillet like Unleavened flatbread, or throw them out.

quiz.q: Why weigh dough instead of cutting it by eye?
choices: So every roll bakes through at the same time
quiz.explain: Small rolls overbake while large ones stay doughy.

quiz.q: Why shape on a bare spot of counter, not on flour?
choices: A little stickiness gives the dough grip to tighten
quiz.explain: On flour, the ball just slides and never builds a tight skin.

knowledge.title: Lean vs. enriched doughs; proofing, under vs. over
body: Proofing is the last rise, after shaping. It decides how a bread turns out more than any other step, and there's no clock for it. You judge it by the dough.

The poke test: flour a fingertip and press it about ½ inch into the side of the dough. If the dent springs back right away, the dough is underproofed. If it springs back slowly and leaves a small dent, it's ready. If it doesn't spring back at all, or the dough sighs and sinks, it's overproofed.
Underproofed bread is dense and tight. It rises hard in the oven and often bursts open along a side, because the yeast still has a lot of gas to give and the gluten is still tight.

Overproofed bread rises too far before baking. The gluten stretches thin and weak, the yeast runs out of sugar, and the loaf collapses or spreads flat in the oven, with big holes under the crust and a sour, boozy smell.

Temperature sets the pace. A warm kitchen (80°F) might proof rolls in 30 minutes; a cool one (68°F) might take an hour and a half. The fridge (below 40°F) slows it to overnight, which is called a cold proof or retarding the dough. That's the make-ahead method in this week's Beyond the Recipe.

quiz.q: You poke the dough and the dent springs right back. What does that mean?
choices: It's underproofed; give it more time
quiz.explain: Ready dough springs back slowly and leaves a small dent.

quiz.q: What does overproofed bread do in the oven?
quiz.explain: The gluten is stretched weak, and the yeast has run out of food.

quiz.q: Why might rolls proof faster on one day than another?
quiz.explain: Yeast works faster when it's warm.

quiz.q: What does a cold proof in the fridge do?
choices: Slows the yeast so dough can wait overnight
quiz.explain: It's also called retarding the dough.

sabbath.title: Shape rolls a day ahead; cold proof overnight
body: A cold proof splits rolls across two days. You do the mixing and shaping one day, and the next day you only bake them. The long, cool rise also gives them more flavor.

The fridge keeps a dough with milk and egg safe, because it stays below 40°F, out of the danger zone. Shaped dough keeps there for 8 to 16 hours. Past about a day, the yeast runs out of food and the rolls overproof.
Shaping a day ahead splits the work in two, so baking day is short.
steps: Make this week's roll dough and let it rise once, as the recipe says.
Weigh, divide, and shape the rolls into the buttered dish.
Cover the dish tightly with plastic wrap or a lid, and put it straight in the fridge. Label it with the time.
Leave it 8 to 16 hours.

The next day, take the dish out and leave it on the counter, still covered, until the rolls are puffy and touching and pass the poke test. This usually takes 1 to 2 hours, because the dough starts cold.
Heat the oven to 375°F and bake them as the recipe says, to 190°F in the middle roll.
Note how the cold-proofed rolls compare with ones made the same day: flavor, rise, and color.

quiz.q: Why is dough with milk and egg safe overnight in the fridge?
choices: It stays below 40°F, out of the danger zone
quiz.explain: Refrigerator temperatures keep it out of the 40–140°F range.

quiz.q: Why do cold rolls need 1 to 2 hours on the counter?
choices: The dough has to warm up and finish proofing
So they don't crack the dish
quiz.explain: Yeast is slow when cold. Use the poke test, not the clock.

drill.title: Cut cold butter in; roll to an even thickness and crimp
body: Three pastry skills, practised on a small dough before the real one: cutting cold butter in to the size of peas, rolling to an even ⅛ inch, and sealing an edge three ways. The practice pies bake into a snack.
Use the flour and butter this week's recipe already buys. If you're making the empanadas, do this drill first so your hands know the repulgue.
steps: Cut 4 tablespoons of cold butter into ½-inch cubes and chill them in the freezer for 10 minutes. Put ¼ cup of water in a cup with ice.

Whisk ¾ cup of flour and a pinch of salt in a bowl. Add the butter and press it in with the back of a fork, tossing, until the biggest pieces are the size of peas. Stop and look: are any pieces still bigger than a pea? Any smeared into a paste?
Sprinkle 2 tablespoons of the ice water over it and toss with the fork. Squeeze a handful. Add water a teaspoon at a time until a squeezed handful just holds. Write down how much water it took.
Press the dough into a disk, cover it, and chill it 20 minutes.

Roll it on a floured counter from the middle out, turning it a quarter turn after each pass. Stop when it's ⅛ inch thick, about as thick as two stacked quarters. Check the edges and the middle with a ruler or your fingertips.
Cut out 6 circles about 3 inches across with a glass or cutter.
Put a teaspoon of jam or cinnamon sugar in the middle of each, wet the edge with water, fold it into a half-moon, and press out the air.
Seal 2 with a fork pressed along the edge, 2 with small folded pleats, and 2 with the repulgue: fold a small piece of the edge over itself and press, then the next, all the way around.
Bake them on a parchment-lined sheet pan at 375°F until golden, about 15 minutes. Let them cool 10 minutes; jam stays very hot.
Which edge held best? Which looked best? Write it down.

quiz.q: How big should the butter be after cutting in?
quiz.explain: Each piece steams into a flaky pocket.

quiz.q: How do you know you've added enough water?
choices: A squeezed handful just holds together
The dough is smooth and sticky
quiz.explain: More water makes a tough crust.

quiz.q: How do you keep the dough the same thickness?
choices: Roll from the middle out, turning a quarter turn each time
Roll back and forth in one direction
quiz.explain: Check the edges and middle as you go.

quiz.q: Why press out the air before sealing?
choices: Trapped air expands in the oven and pops the seal open

knowledge.title: Pastry vs. bread: keeping gluten weak, cold fat, and reading pastry labels
body: Bread and pastry start with the same flour and treat it in opposite ways. Bread wants strong gluten: lots of water and long kneading build a stretchy net that holds gas and rises. Pastry wants weak gluten: little water, cold fat, and a light touch, so it bakes crisp, flaky, and tender instead of chewy.

Fat is what makes pastry. Coated in fat, flour can't soak up as much water, so less gluten forms. Pieces of cold butter left about the size of peas stay solid until the oven, where their water turns to steam and pushes the dough into flaky layers. If the butter warms and smears into the flour, the layers are lost.

Water is added a tablespoon at a time, just until a squeezed handful holds. Then the dough rests in the fridge so the butter firms up and the gluten relaxes. Rolled cold, it doesn't shrink in the oven.

Store-bought crusts, empanada discs, and puff pastry save time, but some are made with fats this app keeps out. Butter, vegetable shortening, and oil are fine. Read the ingredient list every time, because a brand can change its recipe. The list below names what to watch for.
steps: On your phone or at the store, find the ingredient lists for two store-bought pie crusts and one pack of frozen empanada discs or puff pastry.
For each, write down what fat it's made with, and whether it's one your family can use.
Compare the price of one store-bought crust with the cost of the flour and butter in this week's homemade crust.
In your own words, write three ways pastry is made differently from bread, and why each matters.

watch.name: Lard
watch.hides: Fat from pigs. In some store-bought pie crusts, empanada discs, pastry shells, and shortening blends.

watch.name: Suet and beef tallow
watch.hides: The hard fat of cattle and sheep, which Leviticus 3:17 and 7:23 forbid. In some pastry, mincemeat, and shortening blends.

quiz.q: Does pastry want strong gluten or weak gluten?
choices: Weak, for a tender, flaky crust
quiz.explain: Bread wants strong gluten; pastry wants as little as possible.

quiz.q: What makes the flaky layers in pastry?
choices: Cold pieces of butter turning to steam in the oven
quiz.explain: The steam pushes the dough apart.

quiz.q: Why does pastry dough rest in the fridge before rolling?
choices: The butter firms up and the gluten relaxes
quiz.explain: Relaxed dough doesn't shrink in the oven.

quiz.q: A store-bought crust's label lists a fat from the Watch for box. What do you do?
choices: Pick a brand made with butter, shortening, or oil, or make the crust
quiz.explain: Read the list every time; brands change.

sabbath.title: Freeze unbaked pastry
body: Pastry freezes better than almost anything you bake. Freeze it unbaked, and it goes from the freezer straight into the oven, so a warm pie or a pan of empanadas takes only the baking time.
Baking from frozen keeps the butter cold right up until the oven, so the crust is often flakier than one baked fresh. It just needs 5 to 10 minutes more.
There are two ways to keep it: as dough, in disks, or shaped and filled. Anything with a cooked meat filling still has to reach 165°F in the center when it bakes.
steps: Make a double batch of this week's dough, or save part of it.
Dough: press it into 1-inch-thick disks, wrap each tightly in plastic wrap, and put them in a freezer bag. To use one, thaw it overnight in the fridge.
Shaped empanadas or a galette: set them, unbaked and without egg wash, on a parchment-lined sheet pan or plate, not touching, and freeze them until hard, about 2 hours.
Move the frozen empanadas into a freezer bag, or wrap the frozen galette on its parchment in plastic wrap and then foil. Press out the air.
Label everything with what it is, the oven temperature, and the date. Unbaked pastry keeps up to 3 months.
To bake: don't thaw. Brush with egg wash and bake as the recipe says, adding 5 to 10 minutes. Check empanadas for 165°F in the filling, and a galette for thick, bubbling juice and a golden bottom.
Compare one baked from frozen with one baked fresh. Write down any difference in the crust.

quiz.q: Why do empanadas freeze on a pan before going in a bag?
choices: So they freeze separately and don't stick together
quiz.explain: Then you can take out just what you need.

quiz.q: Do you thaw unbaked frozen pastry before baking?
choices: No, bake it from frozen and add 5 to 10 minutes
quiz.explain: Cold butter makes a flakier crust.

quiz.q: What must a frozen meat empanada reach when it bakes?
quiz.explain: Color doesn't tell you the middle is hot.

drill.title: Braid a dough
body: A three-strand braid is the classic challah shape. You'll practice it with a plain dough until it's smooth and even, before you braid this week's challah on your own.
steps: Stir together 1½ cups of all-purpose flour, ½ cup of water, and a pinch of salt. Knead it until it's smooth, about 3 minutes, and cut it into 3 pieces of the same weight.
Roll each piece into a rope about 12 inches long, a little thicker in the middle than at the ends. If a rope shrinks back, let it rest 5 minutes.
Lay the ropes side by side, running away from you, and pinch them together at the far end.
Braid: cross the right rope over the middle one, then the left rope over the new middle one. Keep going, right over middle, left over middle, snug but not stretched.
At the end, pinch the three ropes together and tuck both pinched ends under the loaf.
Unbraid it, roll the ropes again, and braid a second time, this time starting from the middle and working to each end, turning the loaf around between halves. Compare the two: which is more even?
If you have time, try a four-strand or a round braid from a video or book, and note the pattern you used.
Roll the dough out and cook it in a dry skillet like Unleavened flatbread, or throw it out.

quiz.q: In a three-strand braid, where does each outside rope go?
quiz.explain: Right over middle, then left over middle.

quiz.q: Why braid from the middle out to each end?
choices: The loaf comes out even, thick in the middle and tapered
quiz.explain: Braiding end to end tends to leave one end fat and one thin.

knowledge.title: Doneness: color, sound, 190°F inside
body: This week you judge doneness three ways, then take the unit quiz.

Color: the crust browns through the Maillard reaction, where proteins and sugars react above about 300°F. An egg wash, honey, or milk adds proteins and sugars, so enriched breads brown sooner and darker. That's why color alone can fool you.

Sound: tip a loaf over (with oven mitts) and tap the bottom. A done loaf sounds hollow, because the crumb has set and dried. A dull thud means it's still wet inside. It's a useful check, but hard to read on a soft, rich loaf.

Temperature: the thermometer is the sure test. Enriched breads like sandwich loaves, rolls, and challah are done at 190°F in the center. Lean breads (flour, water, yeast, salt) go to about 200 to 210°F for a crisp crust and an open crumb. At these temperatures, the starch has absorbed water and set; this is called gelatinization.
Underbaked bread is gummy and dense in the middle and may sink as it cools. Bread keeps cooking for a while after it comes out, so it's cooled before slicing.

quiz.q: What temperature is an enriched bread done at?
quiz.explain: Lean breads go higher, to about 200 to 210°F.

quiz.q: Why does an egg-washed loaf brown early?
choices: Egg adds proteins and sugars for the Maillard reaction

quiz.q: What does a hollow sound tell you?
choices: The crumb has set and dried
quiz.explain: A dull thud means it's still wet.

quiz.q: Unit review: what water temperature wakes active dry yeast?
quiz.explain: Above about 130°F starts to kill it.

quiz.q: Unit review: which gas raises yeast dough?
quiz.explain: Yeast gives it off as it ferments sugar.

quiz.q: Unit review: what does the windowpane test show?
quiz.explain: The dough stretches thin enough to see light through.

quiz.q: Unit review: a gentle poke springs back slowly and leaves a small dent. The dough is…
quiz.explain: Fast spring-back is under; none at all is over.

quiz.q: Unit review: why is bread kept in the freezer, not the fridge?
choices: The fridge speeds staling; the freezer stops it
The fridge is unsafe for bread
Bread can't be frozen after baking
quiz.explain: Staling is starch recrystallizing, fastest just above freezing.

quiz.q: Unit review: why weigh dough when dividing it?
quiz.explain: Sizes by eye can differ by a third.

sabbath.title: Leaven and unleavened bread (Exodus 12:15–20; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8)
body: Leaven is anything that makes dough rise by fermentation: yeast, or a sourdough starter, a piece of old dough kept back to start the next batch. You've baked with it for four weeks. Scripture uses it in two ways, as a real food and as a picture.

As a food: at the first Passover, Israel left Egypt in such a hurry that their dough had no time to rise (Exodus 12:34, 39). God commanded them to eat unleavened bread for seven days each year, from the evening of the 14th day of the first month to the evening of the 21st, and to put all leaven out of their houses (Exodus 12:15–20). Deuteronomy calls it "the bread of affliction," eaten to remember leaving Egypt in haste (Deuteronomy 16:3).

As a picture: Paul writes, "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6). A pinch of starter works through an entire batch of dough. He uses that to show how one wrong left alone spreads through a whole community, and tells the believers to "celebrate the festival … with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Corinthians 5:8).

Leaven isn't always bad in Scripture. The two loaves offered at the Feast of Weeks were baked with leaven (Leviticus 23:17), and Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to leaven that a woman worked into three measures of flour until all of it rose (Matthew 13:33).
Families keep these days in different ways. This app shows the unleavened days a family sets and plans around leavened recipes on those days.
steps: Read Exodus 12:14–20 and 12:33–39.
Read 1 Corinthians 5:6–8.
Read Leviticus 23:15–17 and Matthew 13:33.
From your own baking, explain in writing how "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" works in a bowl of dough. How much yeast went into your challah, and how much dough did it raise?
Answer in writing: in 1 Corinthians 5, what does leaven stand for, and what does unleavened bread stand for?
Share your answers with an adult over this week's challah.

quiz.q: Why was Israel's bread unleavened when they left Egypt?
choices: They left in haste, before the dough could rise

quiz.q: How many days is unleavened bread eaten in Exodus 12?
What does Paul use leaven to picture in 1 Corinthians 5?
choices: Wrong that spreads through a whole community
quiz.explain: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6).

quiz.q: Which offering was baked with leaven?
choices: The two loaves at the Feast of Weeks
