drill.title: Set up a steamer; steam vegetables to crisp-tender
body: Steamed vegetables go from raw to crisp-tender to soft in a few minutes, and the only way to learn where the line is is to taste. You'll set up a steamer basket, steam two vegetables, and pull a piece out every minute to find the moment each one is right.

Use the carrots and green beans this week's salmon already buys; if you're cooking the steamed fish instead, use 2 carrots and a handful of green beans or a small head of broccoli. An adult is nearby for the stove.
steps: Open the steamer basket in a large pot. Pour in water to just below the basket, not through the holes. Put the lid on and bring it to a boil over high heat.
Peel 2 carrots and cut them into ¼-inch coins. Trim a large handful of green beans.
With oven mitts, lift the lid far edge first, so it shields you from the steam. Spread the carrots in the basket, put the lid back on, and start a timer.
Every minute, lift the lid away from you, take out one carrot coin with tongs, and set it on a plate in a row, in order. Stop at 8 minutes.
Do the same with the green beans, one bean a minute, for 7 minutes.

Let the rows cool for a minute. Taste each piece in order, and press each with a fork. Write down the minute each vegetable turned crisp-tender (bright, with a little bite at the center) and the minute it turned soft and dull.
Check the water: how far did it drop? Write it down, so you know how long an inch of water lasts on your stove.
Turn off the burner and leave the lid on until the pot stops steaming. Eat the vegetables, or keep them for the week's meals.

quiz.q: Where does the water sit in a steamer?
choices: Below the basket, not touching the food
quiz.explain: Food in the water boils instead of steaming.

quiz.q: How do you lift a steaming lid?
choices: Far edge first, so the lid shields you
quiz.explain: The steam goes away from you.

quiz.q: What does crisp-tender look like?
choices: Bright color, with a little bite in the center
quiz.explain: Past it, green vegetables turn olive-gray.

quiz.q: Why test a piece every minute instead of trusting a chart?
choices: Sizes and stoves differ, so tasting is the real test

knowledge.title: How steam cooks: gentle, moist heat; steam burns and lifting a lid away from you
body: Steaming cooks food in the hot vapor above boiling water. The food never touches the water, so it doesn't lose flavor or color into it, and it never gets hotter than about 212°F, so nothing browns, crisps, or burns. That's why steaming is called gentle, moist heat.

Steam carries more heat than you'd think. To turn water into steam takes a large amount of energy, and the steam gives all of it back the moment it touches something cooler and turns back into water. That's why steam cooks food faster than dry oven air at the same temperature, and why it's so good at cooking delicate fish evenly.

It's also why steam burns are so serious. Steam that condenses on your skin delivers far more heat than a splash of water at the same temperature, and a cloud of it can scald your face, wrists, or arms before you feel it. Most steaming burns happen at one moment: when a lid comes off.

So lift a lid by its far edge first, tilting it toward you like a shield, and keep your face back. Use oven mitts on the lid and on metal basket handles, which get as hot as the steam. Open a microwave bowl, a parchment packet, or a bag of steamed vegetables on the side away from you. Don't reach across a steaming pot.

A steamer needs only three things: water below the food, a way to hold the food above it, and a lid. A folding steamer basket, a bamboo steamer over a wok, or a heatproof plate on three balls of foil all work. The water should boil steadily but not so hard that it splashes up into the food, and it needs checking: an inch lasts about 20 minutes. If it runs low, add hot water from a kettle, not cold, so the steaming doesn't stop.

Steaming suits foods that are tender to begin with and that you want to taste plainly: fish, vegetables, dumplings, eggs, and buns. Vegetables cooked this way keep more of the vitamins that dissolve in water, like vitamin C, than boiled ones, because they aren't sitting in the water those vitamins leak into.
Doneness works the same as always. Vegetables are tested with a knife or a taste; fish reads 145°F in the thickest part and flakes; chicken, if you steam it, reads 165°F.
steps: List three foods you've eaten that were steamed. For each, write what held it above the water.
Find a steamer basket, a pot that fits it, and its lid in your kitchen. Practise lifting the cold lid far edge first, with mitts on.
In one sentence, explain to someone at home why steam burns worse than hot water.

quiz.q: What's the hottest steam from boiling water gets in an open pot?
Why does steam cook faster than oven air at the same temperature?
choices: It gives up a lot of heat when it turns back into water
quiz.explain: That same heat is what burns skin.

quiz.q: When do most steaming burns happen?
The water is running low mid-steam. What do you add?
quiz.explain: Hot water keeps the steam going.

quiz.q: Why do steamed vegetables keep more vitamin C than boiled ones?
choices: They don't sit in the water it leaks into
quiz.explain: Water-soluble vitamins leak into cooking water.

sabbath.title: Make a sauce ahead, finish the fish fresh
body: Cooked fish doesn't reheat well: it dries out and its smell gets stronger. But the sauce it cooks in reheats perfectly. So many cooks make the sauce ahead and cook the fish fresh, in minutes, right before eating. Planning this way puts the longest part of the work on the day you have the most time.
A sauce like this week's lemon-dill yogurt or ginger-scallion keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge, covered. Yogurt sauces don't freeze well, so make only what the week needs.
The same idea works for other dishes: a curry sauce ahead, chicken cooked in it fresh; a stir-fry sauce mixed ahead, the stir-fry cooked in minutes.
steps: Make a double batch of this week's sauce.
Store it covered in the fridge, labeled with the date.
Later in the week, take the sauce out while you set up the steamer.
Steam fresh fish until it reads 145°F and flakes, and spoon the sauce over it.
Write down how long the meal took from the fridge to the table.

quiz.q: Why make the sauce ahead but cook the fish fresh?
choices: Cooked fish dries out and smells stronger when reheated
quiz.explain: The sauce reheats well; fish doesn't.

quiz.q: How long does a tomato sauce keep in the fridge?

drill.title: Toast rice in fat; measure by ratio
body: Does toasting really make a difference? You'll cook two small batches of rice exactly the same way, except that one is toasted first, and compare them.
steps: Rinse 1 cup of long-grain white rice until the water is only a little cloudy, and split it into two ½-cup piles.
Batch 1, plain: put ½ cup of rice and ¾ cup of water in a small saucepan with a pinch of salt.

Batch 2, toasted: melt 1 tablespoon of butter or oil in a second small saucepan over medium heat. Add the other ½ cup of rice and stir until the edges of the grains turn see-through and it smells nutty, about 3 minutes. Stand back and add ¾ cup of water heated in the microwave, and a pinch of salt.
Bring both to a boil, then turn them to the lowest heat, put the lids on, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lids. Turn off the heat and rest 10 minutes.
Fluff both with a fork. Compare them side by side: color, smell, stickiness, and taste. Write down which you'd serve and why.
Eat them as a side this week, or cool them safely and keep them in the fridge for up to 4 days.

quiz.q: How do you know the rice is toasted enough?
choices: The edges of the grains turn see-through and it smells nutty

quiz.q: Why does the water go into the toasted rice hot?
choices: So the pan stays at a boil and the rice cooks evenly

knowledge.title: Absorption vs. pasta method; ratios for rice, bulgur, quinoa
body: There are two main ways to cook a grain. In the absorption method, the grain cooks in a measured amount of water and drinks all of it, so nothing is drained. Rice, quinoa, bulgur, and couscous are usually cooked this way. In the pasta method, the grain boils in plenty of water and is drained when it's tender, like pasta. Barley, farro, wild rice, and brown rice cook well this way.

The absorption method needs a ratio: how much liquid for each cup of grain. Rinsed long-grain white rice takes about 1½ cups of water per cup (15 minutes, then a rest). Brown rice takes about 2 cups (45 minutes). Quinoa takes 2 cups (15 minutes), and needs a good rinse first to wash off its bitter coating. Coarse bulgur takes 2 cups (15 minutes). Couscous takes 1¼ cups of boiling water poured over it, with 5 minutes covered off the heat.
The pasta method needs no ratio at all, which makes it forgiving: taste the grain, and drain it when it's done. The cost is the flavor and nutrients that pour down the sink with the water.

A pilaf is the absorption method with one step added: the grain is toasted in fat first. Every grain gets a coat of fat that keeps it separate, and the toasting adds a nutty flavor. Bulgur, orzo, and many other grains can be cooked as a pilaf too.
Whatever the method, keep the lid on and the stirring out once the grain is simmering. Lifting the lid lets out the steam that finishes the cooking, and stirring breaks grains and makes them sticky.

quiz.q: In the absorption method, what happens to the water?
choices: The grain drinks all of it
It boils away with the lid off

quiz.q: About how much water does a cup of rinsed long-grain white rice take?
Why rinse quinoa before cooking it?
choices: To wash off its bitter coating
quiz.explain: The coating tastes soapy and bitter.

quiz.q: What makes a pilaf a pilaf?
choices: The grain is toasted in fat before the liquid
quiz.explain: Toasting coats each grain and adds flavor.

quiz.q: What's the advantage of the pasta method?
choices: No ratio to get right; drain when it's done
quiz.explain: The cost is what pours down the sink.

sabbath.title: Cook grains ahead and reheat them with steam
body: Cooked grains keep well, so a big pot cooked ahead becomes quick meals all week: rice for stir-fries, bulgur for salads, quinoa for bowls. Cook once, and the grain is ready for three or four meals.

Cooked rice needs care, as week 1's danger-zone page taught: its spores survive cooking and grow if it sits warm. Spread hot grains out on a sheet pan to cool fast, and get them into the fridge within an hour. They keep 4 days in the fridge, or 2 to 3 months in the freezer.

Cold grains go hard and dry, because their starch firms up as it chills. Steam brings them back: a little water and a cover. Sprinkle about a tablespoon of water over each cup, cover the dish or pan, and heat until it's steaming hot and reads 165°F. Fluff with a fork.
steps: Cook a double batch of rice, bulgur, or quinoa by its ratio.
Spread it on a sheet pan to cool, then pack it into containers within an hour of cooking. Label them with the grain and the date.
Freeze one container, and keep the rest in the fridge.
Later in the week, reheat a portion with steam: sprinkle on a tablespoon of water per cup, cover it, and heat it in the microwave or a covered pan until it reads 165°F.
Compare it with a portion reheated with no water and no cover. Write down the difference.
Use the rest in a meal this week.

quiz.q: Why do cold grains turn hard and dry?
choices: Their starch firms up as it chills

quiz.q: How soon should cooked rice go into the fridge?
choices: Once it's room temperature, any time
quiz.explain: Spores in rice grow if it sits warm.

drill.title: Quick-soak vs. overnight soak; rinse and pick over lentils
body: You'll soak two batches of the same beans two ways, cook them side by side, and see whether the overnight soak is worth planning for. Start the overnight batch the evening before.
Every bag of dried legumes gets picked over and rinsed before cooking. Then you'll cook red and brown lentils side by side and see why recipes use them so differently.
steps: The evening before: pick over and rinse 1 cup of dried black beans. Put them in a bowl with 4 cups of cold water and leave them overnight.
The next day: pick over and rinse another 1 cup of black beans. Put them in a saucepan with 4 cups of water, boil them for 2 minutes, turn off the heat, put the lid on, and leave them for 1 hour.
Drain both batches and measure them in a measuring cup. Write down how much each one grew, and look at their skins.
Put each batch in its own saucepan with fresh water to cover by 2 inches and a pinch of salt. Bring both to a boil, then simmer gently with the lids slightly open.
From 45 minutes on, taste 3 beans from each pot every 10 minutes, letting them cool first. Write down when each batch is creamy all the way through, and how many split skins each has.
Cool the cooked beans safely and store them in their liquid in the fridge for up to 4 days, for tacos, rice, or soup.
Spread ½ cup of red lentils and ½ cup of brown lentils on two plates. Pick out any tiny stones, clumps of dirt, or shriveled ones. Write down what you found.
Rinse each in a bowl of cold water: swish, pour off the cloudy water while holding the lentils back with your hand, and repeat until the water is almost clear.
Put each in its own saucepan with 2 cups of water. Bring both to a boil, then turn them down to a gentle simmer with the lids off.
Every 5 minutes, scoop out a few of each, let them cool, and taste them. Write down the time each one is tender, and the time the red ones fall apart.
Drain the brown lentils and compare them with the red ones. Which would you use in a soup? Which in a salad or with rice?
Season both with a little salt, olive oil, and lemon and eat them as a side, or store them in the fridge and use them within 4 days.

quiz.q: What's the first step of a quick soak?
quiz.explain: Then they sit covered for an hour.

quiz.q: Why taste three beans, not one?
choices: Beans in one pot don't all cook at the same speed
One is too small to taste
quiz.explain: Every bean you taste should be creamy.

quiz.q: Why pick over dried lentils before cooking them?
choices: To find tiny stones or dirt
quiz.explain: They come straight from the field.

quiz.q: Which lentils would you use in a salad?
choices: Brown lentils, because they hold their shape

knowledge.title: Why beans are soaked; legume types and cook times
body: A dried bean is a seed, sealed up hard and dry so it can wait months to sprout. Soaking wakes it up: overnight in plenty of cold water, a bean drinks about its own weight in water and swells to twice its size.

Soaking makes beans cook faster and more evenly. Unsoaked, the outside of a bean softens and splits long before the middle is done. Soaked, water is already in the middle when the heat starts, so the whole bean cooks together.
Soaking also washes out some of the sugars in beans that people can't digest. Those sugars are what make beans gassy. Pouring off the soaking water and cooking in fresh water helps.

There are two ways. An overnight soak takes 8 to 12 hours in cold water. A quick soak takes about an hour: boil the beans for 2 minutes, turn off the heat, cover them, and leave them. Both work; the overnight soak gives slightly more even beans. Lentils and split peas don't need either.

Red kidney beans need one more step. Raw or undercooked, they contain a natural toxin, and as few as four or five raw beans can make a person very sick. Soaking doesn't remove it. Boiling hard for 10 minutes does, which is why every kidney bean recipe starts with a hard boil. A slow cooker on low may never get hot enough. Canned kidney beans are already cooked and safe.

Legumes are the seeds of plants that grow their seeds in pods: beans, lentils, peas, and chickpeas. Dried, they keep for a year or more in the pantry, and they're one of the cheapest ways to feed a family. They're full of protein and fiber, and eaten with a grain, like beans with rice or lentils with bread, they give the body all the protein building blocks it needs.

Lentils are small and flat and cook fast, with no soak. Red lentils are sold split, with their skins off, and fall apart in 15 to 20 minutes, which is why they make smooth soups. Brown and green lentils keep their skins and hold their shape: 20 to 30 minutes. Split peas take 30 to 45 minutes and melt like red lentils.

Beans and chickpeas are bigger and harder. Soaked overnight, black beans and pinto beans take about 1 to 1½ hours of simmering, red kidney beans about 1½ hours after a 10-minute hard boil, and chickpeas 1½ to 2 hours. Unsoaked, each takes much longer and cooks less evenly.

These times are a guide. Old beans, from the back of the pantry, can take twice as long, so taste a few rather than trusting the clock. Acid slows softening: tomatoes, vinegar, or lemon added too early can keep beans firm for hours, so add them once the beans are tender. Salt in the pot is fine from the start.
Canned beans are already cooked. They're quick and good, but they cost more, and you can't control their texture or salt.

quiz.q: About how big does a bean get after an overnight soak?
quiz.explain: It drinks about its own weight in water.

quiz.q: Why do soaked beans cook more evenly?
choices: Water is already in the middle when the heat starts
quiz.explain: Unsoaked, the outside splits before the middle is done.

quiz.q: How do you quick-soak beans?
choices: Boil 2 minutes, then cover and leave about an hour
Soak them in hot tap water for 10 minutes
quiz.explain: It works nearly as well as overnight.

quiz.q: What makes red kidney beans safe to eat?
choices: Cooking them on low all day
quiz.explain: Soaking doesn't remove the toxin; a hard boil does.

quiz.q: Which of these needs no soak?
quiz.explain: They're small and thin enough to cook through quickly.

quiz.q: Which of these cooks fastest?
quiz.explain: Split and skinless, they're done in 15 to 20 minutes.

quiz.q: Which keep their shape when cooked: red lentils or brown lentils?
When should you add tomatoes or vinegar to a pot of beans?
Your beans are still hard after the usual time. What's the likely reason?
quiz.explain: Old beans can take twice as long.

quiz.q: What does a legume eaten with a grain give you?
choices: All the protein building blocks the body needs
quiz.explain: Like beans with rice, or lentils with bread.

sabbath.title: Daniel's diet (Daniel 1)
body: When Babylon conquered Jerusalem, King Nebuchadnezzar took young men of Judah's royal and noble families to train for his court, among them Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The king gave them a daily portion of the food he ate and the wine he drank (Daniel 1:3–5).

"But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Daniel 1:8). The king's table likely served meat God's law called unclean, or meat not prepared the way the law required, and food and wine offered first to Babylon's gods.

Daniel didn't refuse rudely. He asked the official in charge for permission, and when the official was afraid, he offered a test: "Test your servants for ten days; let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink" (Daniel 1:12). The Hebrew word for vegetables means things grown from seed, which would include grains and legumes like the ones in this unit.

"At the end of ten days it was seen that they were better in appearance and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's food" (Daniel 1:15). God gave the four young men learning and skill, and the king found them ten times better than all the wise men of his kingdom (Daniel 1:17–20).
steps: Read Daniel 1.
Answer in writing: why did Daniel refuse the king's food?
Answer in writing: how did Daniel ask for a change? What can you learn from the way he asked, not just what he asked for?
Plan one day of meals made from foods grown from seed: grains, beans, lentils, vegetables, and fruit. Use at least one dish from this unit.
With your family, cook one of those meals this week, and talk about Daniel 1 while you eat.

quiz.q: What did Daniel ask to eat and drink during the test?
How long was the test?
What does the Hebrew word for "vegetables" in Daniel 1 mean?
quiz.explain: It would include grains and legumes.

drill.title: Skim and strain a stock; cool it fast and lift off the fat
body: A stock is only as clear and useful as its finishing: skimmed, strained, cooled fast, and its fat lifted off. You'll do all four, then see the gelatin set.

Use this week's chicken noodle soup stock: make it as the recipe says with 2 more cups of water, and keep back 2 cups. If you're cooking the arroz caldo instead, make a small stock from 1 pound of chicken wings, a quarter of an onion, a piece of carrot, and 5 cups of cold water, simmered 1½ hours; wash your hands with soap after handling the raw wings. An adult is nearby for the stove and the hot liquid.
steps: While the stock simmers, skim the gray foam off the top with a spoon every 10 minutes. Put each spoonful in a cup and look at it: it's proteins from the chicken, safe but cloudy.
Line a colander with a paper towel, wet it, and set it over a bowl. An adult ladles 2 cups of hot stock through it. Look at what the towel catches.
Fill the sink a few inches deep with cold water and ice. Pour the strained stock into a small metal bowl or a shallow container and set it in the ice water.
Stir it every few minutes and check it with the thermometer. Write down how long it takes to go from steaming hot to 70°F. It should get there well within 2 hours.
Cover it, label it with the date, and put it in the fridge overnight.
The next day, look at the top: the fat has set into a pale layer. Lift it off with a spoon in pieces and keep it in a jar in the fridge for frying, or throw it away.
Tip the container: does the stock under the fat wobble like jelly? Write down how firm it set. That's the gelatin from the skin and joints.
Use the stock within 4 days, or freeze it in 1-cup containers for up to 3 months.

quiz.q: Why cool stock in an ice bath instead of leaving it on the counter?
choices: It has to pass through the danger zone fast
quiz.explain: From hot to 70°F within 2 hours, then into the fridge.

quiz.q: What's the gray foam on simmering stock?
quiz.explain: Skimming it keeps the stock clear.

quiz.q: Why chill stock before taking off the fat?
choices: The fat sets into a layer you can lift off
quiz.explain: Warm fat is hard to skim all of.

quiz.q: What makes cold stock set like jelly?
quiz.explain: A good set means a rich stock.

knowledge.title: Stock vs. broth; why simmer, not boil; gelatin
body: Stock and broth are both made by simmering in water, and people use the words loosely, but cooks mean different things. A stock is made mostly from bones, skin, and joints, with a few vegetables, and no salt. It's an ingredient, the base for soups, sauces, rice, and braises. A broth is made mostly from meat, is seasoned, and is good enough to drink on its own. "Bone broth" on a label is a name for a long-simmered stock.

What gives a stock its body is gelatin. Bones, skin, and joints are held together by collagen, a tough protein. Held near a simmer for hours, collagen melts into gelatin, which dissolves in the water. A stock rich in gelatin feels silky in your mouth and sets like jelly when cold. Wings, backs, necks, and feet are the best parts for it; a lean breast gives almost none.

Stocks simmer; they don't boil. A rolling boil churns the fat and the cloudy proteins into the liquid as tiny drops, and they stay there: the stock turns cloudy and tastes greasy. At a bare simmer, with a bubble breaking now and then, the fat rises to the top and the proteins clump into foam you can skim. Starting from cold water helps the same way, because the proteins release slowly.

How long depends on the bones. Fish bones give their flavor in 30 to 45 minutes and turn bitter after that. Chicken takes 1½ to 3 hours. Beef bones, which are big and dense, take 4 to 6, and are often roasted first for a deep brown stock.

Stocks aren't salted because they're used in so many ways: cooked down into a sauce, absorbed by rice, reduced for a soup. Salt doesn't cook away, so a salted stock can end up far too salty. Season the dish you make with it.

Store-bought broth and stock save hours. Their labels vary a lot in salt, so check, and buy low-sodium when you can so you can season it yourself. Read the ingredient list too: bouillon cubes and powders, and some seafood or "dashi" bases, can carry ingredients from animals your family doesn't eat.
steps: Find a carton of broth or stock at home or at the store. Copy its ingredient list and its sodium per cup.
Compare it with this week's homemade stock: which has more salt? Which set like jelly in the fridge?
Write the difference between a stock and a broth in your own words.

quiz.q: What's the main difference between a stock and a broth?
choices: Stock is mostly bones and unsalted; broth is mostly meat and seasoned
quiz.explain: Stock is an ingredient; broth can be served alone.

quiz.q: Where does gelatin come from?
choices: Collagen in bones, skin, and joints, melted by long simmering
quiz.explain: Wings and backs give the most.

quiz.q: Why does a boiled stock turn cloudy?
choices: The boil churns fat and proteins into tiny drops in the liquid
quiz.explain: Keep it at a bare simmer.

quiz.q: Why isn't stock salted?
choices: It may be cooked down, and salt doesn't cook away

quiz.q: About how long does chicken stock simmer?
quiz.explain: Fish takes less; beef takes more.

sabbath.title: Soup that improves when made ahead; freeze it in portions
body: Soup is one of the best things to freeze. A batch made ahead and frozen in portions turns into several quick meals later. A few portions in the freezer mean a hot meal on a busy night is only a reheat away.
Cool it first: from 140°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 40°F within 4 more, in shallow containers, before it goes in the freezer. A hot pot in the freezer warms everything around it.
Liquids grow as they freeze. Leave about an inch of space at the top of every container, or it can crack or pop its lid. Freezer bags laid flat freeze fast and stack like books.

Most bean, lentil, and vegetable soups keep their best for 2 to 3 months. Soups with pasta or potatoes go soft, and soups with cream or milk can separate, so freeze those before the pasta or cream goes in. Thaw a portion in the fridge overnight and reheat it to 165°F, adding water, because lentil soups thicken as they sit.
steps: Make a double batch of this week's chicken noodle soup or arroz caldo, or set half of it aside.
Cool it safely and check it reaches 40°F.
Ladle it into freezer containers or bags in 1- or 2-person portions, leaving an inch of space at the top.
Label each with the soup's name and the date, and freeze bags flat on a sheet pan until solid, then stand them up.
Later in the week, thaw one portion in the fridge overnight and reheat it on the stove to 165°F, with a splash of water.
Write down how it compared with the fresh soup, and how long the frozen meal took.

quiz.q: Why leave space at the top of a container of soup for the freezer?
quiz.explain: A full container can crack or pop its lid.

quiz.q: What temperature does thawed soup need to reach when you reheat it?

drill.title: Poach an egg; steam a vegetable without a recipe
body: Two skills without a recipe in front of you. A poached egg is cooked in water held just below a simmer, and you'll judge it by the thermometer and by the white. Then you'll steam a vegetable from start to finish on your own, using what you learned in week 16.
Use 4 eggs and one vegetable from this week's shopping: the bell peppers, or a carrot if you have one. An adult is nearby for the stove.
steps: Fill a wide saucepan with 3 inches of water and heat it over medium. Use the thermometer: hold it at 180 to 190°F, with small bubbles on the bottom and only a few rising.
Crack one egg into a small cup. Wash your hands with soap.
Lower the cup to the water and tip the egg in gently. Set a timer for 4 minutes.

Lift it out with a slotted spoon and press the white with a fingertip: it should be completely set, and the yolk soft but thickened. If the white is still clear anywhere, lower it back for 1 more minute.
Poach the other 3 eggs, two at a time, and write down your time and water temperature for the best one.
Now the vegetable: set up the steamer, cut the vegetable into even pieces, and steam it, testing with a fork until it's crisp-tender. Write down your cut size and the time it took.
Eat the eggs and vegetable while they're hot, and turn off the stove.

quiz.q: What temperature is poaching water held at?
quiz.explain: A hard boil shreds the white.

quiz.q: How do you know a poached egg's white is done?
choices: It's completely set, with no clear parts
quiz.explain: Then the yolk is soft but thickened.

quiz.q: Why tip the egg in from a cup, close to the water?
choices: It slides in gently and holds together
quiz.explain: Dropped from high, the white spreads out.

quiz.q: What's the test for a steamed vegetable without a recipe?
choices: A fork or taste: bright, with a little bite
quiz.explain: Your own times from week 16 help.

knowledge.title: Soup families: clear, thick, puréed
body: Most of the world's soups fall into three families, by how they get their body.

Clear soups are a well-made stock or broth with things cooked in it: chicken noodle soup, Vietnamese phở, egg drop soup, Mexican caldo de res, Greek avgolemono. Everything depends on the stock, so it's skimmed, strained, and kept from boiling.

Thick soups get their body from a starch or a cream. The starch can be a roux of flour and fat (cream of mushroom, corn chowder), potatoes (potato leek), rice cooked until it breaks down (arroz caldo, congee), or pasta and beans (minestrone, pasta e fagioli). Thick soups need stirring, because starch catches on the bottom, and they keep thickening as they stand.

Puréed soups are cooked vegetables or legumes blended smooth: butternut squash, tomato, black bean, split pea, red lentil. Most need no flour at all; the vegetable is the thickener. An immersion blender purées right in the pot. A countertop blender works too, filled only halfway with the lid vented and a towel over it, because hot liquid expands and can blow the lid off.

A stew is not a soup. A stew has more solid food than liquid, cut in bigger pieces, and the liquid is a sauce rather than something you sip. This week's moqueca is a stew; this week's meatballs simmer in a sauce, not a soup.

Whatever the family, finish a soup by tasting it hot, the way it'll be eaten, and correcting it: salt if it tastes flat, an acid like lemon or vinegar if it tastes heavy, and water or stock if it's grown too thick.
steps: Write each of these soups under its family: chicken noodle, potato leek, black bean, egg drop, minestrone, butternut squash, arroz caldo, phở.
For each thick soup, write what thickens it.
Plan a soup your family would like, name its family, and write its four or five main ingredients.

quiz.q: Which family is chicken noodle soup in?
quiz.explain: A clear stock with things cooked in it.

quiz.q: What thickens arroz caldo?
choices: Rice breaking down as it simmers

quiz.q: Why fill a blender only halfway with hot soup?
choices: Hot liquid expands and can blow the lid off
quiz.explain: Vent the lid and hold a towel over it.

quiz.q: What's the difference between a stew and a soup?
choices: A stew has more solids than liquid, and the liquid is a sauce

quiz.q: A finished soup tastes heavy. What do you add?
choices: An acid, like lemon or vinegar
quiz.explain: Flat needs salt; heavy needs acid.

sabbath.title: Hospitality: Abraham's meal for his guests (Genesis 18:1–8; Hebrews 13:2)
body: Genesis 18 opens with Abraham sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, by the oaks of Mamre. He looked up and saw three men standing nearby. "When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth" (Genesis 18:2). The chapter tells us that the LORD Himself had come to Abraham, though Abraham hadn't yet been told who his guests were.

Abraham offered them very little: "Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree, while I bring a morsel of bread" (Genesis 18:4–5). Then he hurried. He told Sarah to bake cakes from three seahs of fine flour, about 20 quarts, far more than three guests could eat. He ran to the herd himself, picked a calf "tender and good," and had it prepared quickly. He brought curds and milk with it, "and he stood by them under the tree while they ate" (Genesis 18:6–8).

Look at how he served. He ran, though it was the hottest part of the day and he was an old man. He promised a little and gave a feast. He chose the best of what he had. And he didn't sit down and eat first: he stood by, ready to serve his guests.

The New Testament points back to this meal: "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Hebrews 13:2). Hospitality in the Bible isn't a party for friends; it's welcoming whoever comes, and caring for them with your best.

Soup and stew have always been hospitality food. They stretch to feed one more, they hold warm until a guest arrives, and they can be made ahead with care. This unit's cooking is the kind that welcomes people.
steps: Read Genesis 18:1–8 and Hebrews 13:2.
Answer in writing: what did Abraham promise his guests, and what did he give them?
Answer in writing: name three things Abraham did that showed care for his guests, besides the food.
With your family, invite someone to a meal: a neighbor, a friend, or someone new. Cook one dish from this unit for them.
When they come, serve them first, and make sure they have what they need before you sit down.

quiz.q: What did Abraham first offer his guests?
choices: A little water and a morsel of bread
quiz.explain: Genesis 18:4–5. Then he gave far more.

quiz.q: What did Abraham do while his guests ate?
choices: He stood by them under the tree

quiz.q: What does Hebrews 13:2 say some have done by showing hospitality?

drill.title: Sweat vs. brown onions side by side; the shimmer test
body: Same onion, same pan, two kinds of heat. You'll cook two batches side by side and taste the difference.
steps: Dice an onion into ¼-inch cubes and divide it into two separate piles.

Sweat the first onion pile: warm 1 tablespoon of oil in a skillet over medium-low heat, add the onion and a pinch of salt, and stir every minute or so for 10 minutes. If you see brown, turn the heat down. Move it to a bowl.

Brown the second onion pile: wipe out the pan, add another tablespoon of oil, and heat it over medium-high until it shimmers. Add the onion, spread it out, and stir only every 2 minutes for 10 to 12 minutes, until it's deep golden brown in spots. If any edges turn black, turn the heat down. Move it to a second bowl.
Look at the pan after each batch. Which one left brown bits stuck to the bottom?
Let both cool a little and taste them side by side. Write down the color, the texture, and the taste of each. Which is sweeter? Which tastes deeper or roastier?
Store both in labeled containers in the fridge for up to 4 days. Use them in eggs, on a sandwich, or stirred into rice.

quiz.q: Why add a pinch of salt to the sweating onion?
choices: It pulls out water, so the onion softens without browning
quiz.explain: Salt draws water out of vegetables.

quiz.q: Which batch leaves brown bits on the pan?
quiz.explain: Those brown bits are fond, and week 25's drill uses them.

knowledge.title: Browning, and smoke points of common oils
body: A seared burger tastes different from a boiled one, and toast tastes different from bread. The difference is browning, and it comes from chemical reactions that only happen at high heat.

The biggest one is the Maillard reaction, named for Louis-Camille Maillard, the French chemist who described it in 1912. Above about 300°F, the proteins and sugars on the surface of food react and make hundreds of new flavors and smells: savory, roasty, and meaty. They also make the brown color. It's what browns meat, bread crust, roasted coffee, and the outside of a pancake.

Caramelization is a different reaction. It needs only sugar, heated to about 320°F or more, which breaks down into sweet, nutty, slightly bitter flavors. Onions cooked low and long brown partly this way, because they're full of sugar.

Water stops browning. Water boils at 212°F, and while the surface of food is wet, it can't get any hotter than that, far below the 300°F that browning needs. That's why you pat meat dry, heat the pan first, leave room between pieces, and don't stir too often: each of those lets the surface dry out and get hot.

Brown is flavor; black is burnt. Burnt food tastes bitter, and so do burnt bits stuck to the pan. Sweating is the opposite choice: lower heat and a pinch of salt draw the water out of vegetables, so they soften and turn sweet without browning. A recipe picks one on purpose: sweated vegetables for a gentle, sweet base, and browned ones, or browned meat, for deep, roasty flavor.

body: Before you cook the whole recipe, practice the one hard part on a single fillet: crisp skin that lets go of the pan on its own. Use the first fillet of this week's recipe, so nothing extra is needed, and cook the rest once you've seen how it goes.

sabbath.title: Firstfruits and tithing (Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Proverbs 3:9)
body: God's law sets apart three tithes, each a tenth of our increase, and we still keep them today. The first tithe is the LORD's: "it is holy to the LORD" (Leviticus 27:30). In Israel it went to the Levites, who served at the tabernacle and had no land of their own (Numbers 18:21, 24).

Deuteronomy 14 describes the second tithe: "You shall tithe all the yield of your seed that comes from the field year by year" (Deuteronomy 14:22). The family keeps this tithe and spends it at the place God chooses, at His feasts, eating and rejoicing before Him, "that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It can be turned into money and spent there "for whatever you desire" to eat and rejoice together with your household (Deuteronomy 14:24–26). The Levite is not to be forgotten (Deuteronomy 14:27).

Every third year there is a third tithe as well, in addition to the other two. Families still keep the feasts with their second tithe, and they set aside another tenth for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, "and they shall eat and be filled" (Deuteronomy 14:28–29).
Proverbs puts it simply: "Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce" (Proverbs 3:9). The first and best goes to God, not what's left over.
steps: Read Leviticus 27:30 and Numbers 18:21–24.
Read Deuteronomy 14:22–29.
Read Proverbs 3:9–10.
Answer in writing: what are the three tithes, and what is each one for?
Answer in writing: how does the second tithe teach a family to fear the LORD?
With your family, talk about how you set aside your tithes. Plan one dish from this year's units you'd like to cook or share at the feast with your second tithe, and write it down.

choices: Keeping God's feasts at the place He chooses, with your household

sabbath.title: Dishes that serve well cold
body: Some dishes taste just as good cold as hot, so they can be made a day ahead and set out with no cooking at all: baked fish with a cool sauce, grain salads, lentil and bean salads. A cold meal like this needs no cooking when it's served. Many families plan one for the Sabbath so they can focus on resting.

Cold food stays safe this way: cooked food is cooled and in the fridge within 2 hours, kept at 40°F or colder until it's served, and put back within 2 hours of coming out (1 hour on a hot day over 90°F).
Cold dulls flavor, so a dish meant to be eaten cold needs a little more salt and a squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar. Taste it cold, not warm, before you serve it.

Put everything back in the fridge within 2 hours of setting it out.

sabbath.title: A braise that's better the next day
body: Many sauces, stews, and braises taste better the day after they're made. Overnight, the flavors spread evenly through the sauce and the meat, and the sharp edges soften. Many families cook a big pot like this before the Sabbath, so the next day they only reheat it and can focus on resting.

Cool it safely: from 140°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 40°F within 4 more. Don't put a big, hot pot straight in the fridge; it stays warm in the middle for hours. Divide it into shallow containers, no more than 2 inches deep.
As it chills, fat rises to the top and hardens. You can lift it off with a spoon before you reheat.
A meat sauce keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge, or 3 to 4 months in the freezer. Reheat it on the stove, stirring, with a splash of water if it's thick, until it reads 165°F in the middle.
steps: Make a double batch of this week's chile verde or adobo, or set half of it aside before serving.
Divide it into shallow containers. Let them sit uncovered until the steam stops, then cover them and put them in the fridge within 2 hours of cooking.
Label each container with what it is and the date.
The next day, lift off any hardened fat. Reheat one portion on the stove, stirring, until it reads 165°F in the middle.
Taste it, and write down how it's different from the day you made it.
Freeze any extra in portions, labeled, and use it within 3 months.

drill.title: Timed brunoise
body: A brunoise shows every flaw in your knife work. Today you time it, then check it.
steps: Hone your chef's knife and set the board on a damp towel.
Start a timer. Peel one carrot, square it into a block, and cut ⅛-inch planks, then ⅛-inch julienne, then ⅛-inch cubes.
Stop the timer and write down the time.
Spread 20 cubes on the board and measure a few with a ruler. Note how many are within a hair of ⅛ inch.
Repeat with a second carrot and compare the time and the count.
Weigh the trim and the brunoise. Save the trim for stock.
Use the brunoise in this week's fried rice or ratatouille.

quiz.q: What comes before a brunoise?
Which matters first, speed or evenness?
Why square the carrot into a block?
choices: Flat sides make even planks and it can't roll
quiz.explain: And the trim goes to stock.

knowledge.title: Cuts by size: brunoise, small dice, batonnet, chiffonade; the French herb base
body: Professional recipes name cuts by size, so every cook produces the same piece. Learn them as numbers.
Brunoise: ⅛-inch cubes, cut from a julienne. Small dice: ¼-inch cubes, cut from a batonnet. Medium dice: ½ inch. Large dice: ¾ inch.
Julienne: ⅛ by ⅛ inch, 2 to 2½ inches long. Batonnet: ¼ by ¼ inch, 2½ to 3 inches long. Chiffonade: leafy herbs or greens stacked, rolled tight, and sliced across into thin ribbons.
Precision isn't decoration. Pieces of one size cook in the same time, so a pan of brunoise is done all at once, and a sauce built on it is smooth.

French cooking builds on two aromatic foundations. Mirepoix is onion, carrot, and celery in a 2:1:1 ratio by weight, diced to suit the cooking time: brunoise for a quick sauce, large dice for a long stock. Herbs come as a bouquet garni, a bundle of thyme, bay leaf, and parsley stems tied together so it can be lifted out, or as fines herbes, parsley, chives, tarragon, and chervil, chopped fine and added at the end.
Speed comes from repetition, not hurry. Keep the claw, let the blade do the work, and keep each cut the same before you try to make it faster.

A small dice is cut from which stick?

choices: So it can be lifted out

quiz.explain: Delicate herbs lose flavor with long cooking.

quiz.q: Why cut to an exact size?
choices: Pieces of one size cook in the same time

sabbath.title: Prep every vegetable for a weekend meal
body: A weekend meal is easier to serve when every vegetable is cut beforehand. Done right, the day itself is only cooking.

Most firm vegetables keep 3 to 4 days cut: onions, carrots, celery, peppers, and squash, in sealed containers lined with paper towel. Tomatoes, cucumbers, potatoes, apples, and herbs are cut on the day, or held as noted: potatoes under cold water for up to a day, herbs whole in a damp towel.

Cut the keeping vegetables to the sizes the recipes need, each in its own lined container.
Label each with the recipe, the cut, and the date.
Write a short note of what's left to cut on the day, and how long it will take.
After the meal, note what worked and what you'd change.

drill.title: Weigh vs. measure; weigh the trim to find the yield
body: Today you'll see the difference between measuring and weighing with your own numbers, then find a real yield.
steps: Scoop 1 cup of flour three ways: scooped and packed, spooned and leveled, and sifted in. Weigh each and write it down.
Measure 1 cup of water and weigh it. It should be close to 8⅓ ounces.
Weigh a whole onion. Peel it, trim the root and top, and weigh it again. Work out the yield.
Do the same with a bell pepper: weigh, core and seed, weigh again.
Compare your yields with the Knowledge page's typical numbers.
Keep the trim for stock.

knowledge.title: Why weight beats volume; trim loss and buying enough
body: A cup is a volume, and how much fits in it depends on how it's filled. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from 4¼ to 5¼ ounces; a cup of chopped onion varies more. An ounce is an ounce.
That's why professional kitchens weigh. A scale gives the same result every time, in any hands, and it lets you scale a recipe by multiplication without converting cups and spoons.

Weight also tells you what you're really getting. Yield is the usable weight divided by the bought weight. Typical yields: onions about 90 percent after peeling; bell peppers 80 to 85; carrots 85 to 90; boneless steak trimmed 85 to 90; and meat loses another 20 to 30 percent of its trimmed weight in cooking.

To buy enough, work backward: the plated weight you need, divided by the yield. For 4 servings of 5 ounces of cooked steak (20 ounces) at a 75 percent cooking yield, you need about 27 ounces trimmed, and at 88 percent trim yield, about 30 ounces (1⅞ pounds) as bought.
Small amounts of salt, spices, and leaveners are still often given in spoons, because home scales aren't precise below about a tenth of an ounce.

quiz.q: Why weigh instead of using cups?
choices: An ounce is the same every time

Dry ingredients can be weighed days ahead. Raw meat can be trimmed and portioned up to 2 days ahead in the fridge, or frozen; keep it sealed, on the bottom shelf, away from anything eaten raw.
steps: Pick a recipe for the weekend and convert its main ingredients to weights in ounces and pounds.
Weigh each dry ingredient into a labeled container or bag.
Trim and portion any meat, weigh each portion, and seal it. Wash your hands, board, and knife afterward.
Store the meat on the bottom shelf of the fridge, or freeze it.
Label everything with the recipe, the weight, and the date.
When you cook, note how much time it saved.

knowledge.title: Scaling factors, and what doesn't scale: salt, spice, time, pan size
body: The scaling factor is the servings you want divided by the servings written. From 4 to 12, it's 3. From 6 to 4, it's about 0.67. Multiply every ingredient by it, and round counted items sensibly.
Weights scale cleanly. Volumes do too, but convert awkward results: ⅓ cup × 3 is 1 cup; 1 teaspoon × 3 is 1 tablespoon; 3 tablespoons × 3 is ½ cup plus 1 tablespoon.

Some things don't scale in a straight line. Salt, spices, and chile heat build faster in a big batch: start at about three quarters of the full factor, then taste. Liquids that evaporate, like a simmering sauce, need less than the full factor, because a bigger pot loses less in proportion. Leaveners in baking are often scaled a little under.
Time doesn't multiply. A pot of soup three times the size takes longer to come to a boil, but simmers about the same. Baking time stays the same per pan, as long as the pans are the same size.
Pans don't stretch. A tripled recipe needs three pans of the original size, or one pan with three times the area, at the same depth. Check the oven fits them, and rotate them halfway.

How should salt be scaled up?

knowledge.title: Planning a meal backward from serving time
body: Every meal has a fixed point: the moment it's served. Plan from there backward.
List every component with its active time, hands busy, and its passive time, waiting. A roast might be 15 minutes active and 90 passive; a salad 15 active and nothing passive.
Place each component so it finishes at serving time, counting resting and holding: meat rests 10 minutes, rice holds covered for 20, and dressed greens wilt within minutes, so they go last.

Now check for collisions. Two jobs needing your hands at once, or two pans needing the same burner or the oven at different temperatures, must be moved. Passive time is when you do the active work of something else.
Add slack: 10 to 15 percent of the total, at the start. Write the plan as clock times, not durations, and keep it in view while you cook.

What is passive time?
What goes last?
How much slack should you add?

sabbath.title: Plan a Sabbath prep timeline
body: A Sabbath meal is cooked before the Sabbath begins and served without last-minute work. That makes the timeline run backward from sundown on Friday, with food held hot or served cold.
steps: Choose the Sabbath menu and note which dishes are served hot and which cold.
Mark sundown on Friday as your fixed point.
List every component, with its active and passive time and how it will be held.
Spread the work over Thursday and Friday so Friday afternoon isn't crowded.
Write the timeline as days and clock times, with slack before sundown.
After the meal, note what you'd move, and keep the plan.

Why spread the work over two days?

drill.title: Make mayonnaise, break it, and rescue it
body: Make a mayonnaise, break it on purpose, and bring it back. Once you've rescued one, a broken sauce stops being a disaster. Use pasteurized eggs, and cook the yolk to 160°F first, as this week's recipes do.
steps: Whisk 1 pasteurized egg yolk with 1 teaspoon of lemon juice and 1 teaspoon of water in a heatproof bowl over barely simmering water until it thickens and probes 160°F. Wash your hands after separating the egg.
Off the heat, whisk for a minute to cool it, then add ½ teaspoon of mustard and a pinch of salt.
Measure ¾ cup of neutral oil. Whisk in the first quarter drop by drop, then the rest in a thin stream. Note when it turns thick and pale.
Take a third of the finished mayonnaise into a second bowl. Pour 3 tablespoons of oil in at once and whisk. Watch it break into a greasy, curdled pool.
Rescue it: in a clean bowl, whisk 1 teaspoon of mustard with 1 teaspoon of water. Whisk the broken mayonnaise in a teaspoon at a time until it's thick again.
Compare the two by look and taste, and write down what broke it and what saved it.
Keep the mayonnaise in a covered jar in the fridge and use it within 4 days, in this week's Caesar or ensaladilla.

quiz.q: What breaks a mayonnaise?
choices: Oil added faster than the emulsion can take it
quiz.explain: The droplets merge and the oil separates.

quiz.q: How do you rescue a broken mayonnaise?
choices: Whisk it slowly into a fresh emulsifier
quiz.explain: Mustard and water, or a fresh cooked yolk, then the broken sauce a little at a time.

knowledge.title: Emulsions, and raw eggs: the USDA guideline and pasteurized eggs
body: An emulsion is one liquid dispersed through another as droplets: oil droplets in a water-based liquid in mayonnaise and vinaigrette, water droplets in fat in butter. The two phases don't mix, so an emulsion needs energy (whisking breaks the oil into droplets) and an emulsifier, a molecule with a water-loving end and a fat-loving end that coats each droplet and keeps it from merging with its neighbors.

Egg yolk is the strongest emulsifier in the kitchen. Its lecithin and proteins hold a mayonnaise stable for days, and one yolk can carry well over a cup of oil. Mustard is weaker but useful: it steadies a vinaigrette for an hour instead of a minute. Without an emulsifier, a vinaigrette is a temporary emulsion that separates as soon as you stop.

Three things break an emulsion: oil added faster than there are droplets to hold it, too much oil for the emulsifier (more than about 1½ cups to a yolk), and temperature, since a very cold or a warm sauce loses its grip. The fix is always the same: start a fresh emulsifier and whisk the broken sauce into it slowly.

Now the eggs. Salmonella Enteritidis can be inside an intact, clean egg, passed from the hen before the shell forms, so washing doesn't remove it. The USDA and FDA advise against eating raw or undercooked eggs and say to cook egg dishes to 160°F. The risk is highest for young children, older adults, pregnant women, and anyone with a weakened immune system.

For recipes that use eggs raw, the USDA's answer is pasteurized eggs: in-shell eggs heated in a water bath just enough to kill Salmonella without cooking them, or pasteurized liquid egg products. Store-bought mayonnaise is made with pasteurized eggs and enough acid to be shelf-stable until opened.

This app keeps one standard for every egg: 160°F. So the Level 4 recipes use pasteurized eggs and still cook the yolks to 160°F with the lemon juice before the oil goes in. Cooked this way, the yolk keeps its emulsifying power, and the sauce is safe for every guest at the table.
Homemade mayonnaise and egg-based dressings have no preservatives. Keep them covered in the fridge at 40°F or below and use them within 4 days.

sabbath.title: Make a dressing ahead
body: A dressing made ahead turns a week of salads, wraps, and grain bowls into assembly. Most keep well, but not equally.

A plain vinaigrette of oil, vinegar, salt, and mustard keeps up to 2 weeks in the fridge. Add fresh garlic, shallot, or herbs and the clock shortens to about 4 days: fresh garlic held in oil is a botulism risk if it's left out, so it stays cold and gets used soon. An egg- or dairy-based dressing, like this week's Caesar or a yogurt dressing, keeps 3 to 4 days.
Olive oil firms up in the fridge. Take the jar out 15 minutes before you need it, or run it under warm water, and shake it hard; it re-emulsifies in seconds.
steps: Plan four meals this week that use a dressing.
Make a double batch of a vinaigrette, with mustard, and a single batch of a creamy dressing: this week's Caesar or a yogurt dressing.
Jar each one, and label it with the name, the date made, and the use-by date from the guide above.
Store them on a fridge shelf, not the door, where the temperature swings.
Use them through the week, and note which held up and which didn't.

drill.title: Hold a cold platter below 41°F; the 2-hour rule
body: Run a cold-holding test before you hold food for guests. You'll set out two identical plates, one on ice and one not, and log both for 2 hours.
steps: Chill two plates and a sheet pan of ice packs or frozen water for 30 minutes.
Cut two equal sets of perishable food from the fridge: cheese cubes, cut tomato, and a scoop of a dip.
Set one plate on the ice tray and one on the counter. Probe the cheese on each and log the time and temperature.
Probe both every 30 minutes for 2 hours. Note the room temperature too.
Graph or table your readings. When did the counter plate pass 41°F? Did the iced plate ever?
Discard the counter plate's food at 2 hours. Refrigerate the iced plate's food only if every reading was 41°F or below.

What happens to food left off ice for 2 hours?
choices: It goes back in the fridge

knowledge.title: Food safety for a cold buffet
body: A buffet is the riskiest way to serve food: it sits out, many hands reach in, and nobody is watching the clock. Food safety codes call the risky foods TCS, time/temperature control for safety: anything moist and protein-rich or cut, where bacteria can grow. On a cold table that means sliced meats, cheeses, dips like hummus and labneh, cut tomatoes and melons, leafy greens, cooked grains and beans, and anything with mayonnaise.

Cold holding has a number: 41°F or below, from the FDA Food Code that restaurants follow (your home fridge should run at 40°F or below). There are two ways to control it. Temperature: on ice, probed and logged, with nothing above 41°F. Or time: off ice, out for no more than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F, then discarded, not returned to the fridge.

Cooked food headed for a cold table has to get cold fast. The rule is two-stage cooling: from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F within the next 4. Big, deep containers can't do it; the middle stays warm for hours. Spread food shallow, under 2 inches, and leave it uncovered until it's cool.

Listeria is the cold table's special concern. It grows even at fridge temperature and is found in deli meats and soft cheeses. It's most dangerous during pregnancy and for older adults, which is one more reason cold food stays cold and isn't held for days.

Good buffet practice: small platters, refilled from the fridge on clean plates, never topped up with fresh food on top of old; a separate serving utensil for every dish; bread off the ice and away from the dips; and a written log of times and temperatures. At the end, food that held at 41°F on ice can be refrigerated; anything else is thrown away.
This is a professional's standard, and it's what lets you feed a crowd without making anyone sick.

What are the two ways to control a cold buffet?

sabbath.title: Hospitality: Abraham's meal for his guests (Genesis 18:1–8; Hebrews 13:2)
body: Abraham was sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day when he saw three men standing nearby. He ran to meet them, bowed, and begged them to stay: "Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree, while I bring a morsel of bread" (Genesis 18:4–5).

The "morsel" was a feast. Abraham hurried to Sarah, who made cakes from three seahs of fine flour, enough for a crowd. He ran to the herd himself, chose a calf, "tender and good," and a young man hurried to prepare it. He set it before them with curds and milk, and stood by them under the tree while they ate (Genesis 18:6–8). The guests were the LORD and two angels, though Abraham welcomed them before he knew it.

The New Testament remembers this scene: "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Hebrews 13:2). Paul tells believers to "seek to show hospitality" (Romans 12:13), and Peter adds, "without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9).

Notice what Abraham did: he ran, he offered his best rather than his leftovers, he served the guests himself, and he stayed with them while they ate. Hospitality was a matter of the heart, and also of planning and work.
steps: Read Genesis 18:1–8 and Hebrews 13:1–2.
Read Romans 12:13 and 1 Peter 4:9.
Answer in writing: list every action Abraham took, from seeing the guests to standing by them. What does each show?
Answer in writing: what's the difference between hosting to impress and hosting as Abraham did?
With your family, plan a meal for a guest this month: someone new, alone, or in need. Write the menu from your Unit 1 and 2 recipes, the shopping list, and the budget.
If you can, host it, and use this week's cold-holding skills for anything set out.

choices: A feast of cakes, a tender calf, curds, and milk

quiz.q: According to Hebrews 13:2, who have some entertained unawares?

drill.title: Break a chicken into 8 pieces; save the back for stock
body: A whole chicken breaks into eight serving pieces with nothing but a sharp chef's knife and a feel for the joints. Do it once slowly, naming each joint as you find it, then again for time. Use the pieces in this week's recipe.
steps: Set up: the raw-meat board on a damp towel, a sharp chef's knife, a sheet pan for the pieces, a bag for the back, and hot, soapy water ready. Don't rinse the bird.

Legs: lay the chicken breast up. Pull a leg away from the body, slice through the skin between leg and breast, then bend the leg back until the hip joint pops out. Cut through the joint, scooping the chicken oyster (the round pocket of meat on the back) out with the thigh. Repeat.
Split each leg: skin side down, find the line of fat over the knee joint, and cut straight down through it into drumstick and thigh.
Wings: pull each wing out, find the shoulder joint by wiggling it, and cut through.
Back: stand the bird on its neck end and cut down through the ribs on both sides, separating the breast from the back.
Breast: lay it skin side up and cut through the breastbone, just off center, into two halves. For four breast pieces, halve each across.
Line up the 8 pieces and the back. Weigh the pieces and the back separately, and note both.
Bag and freeze the back (Beyond the Recipe). Wash the knife, board, and pan, wipe the counter and the faucet, and wash your hands.
Next time, time yourself. A cook who knows the joints takes under 5 minutes.

quiz.q: How do you find where to cut a leg off?
choices: Bend it back until the hip joint pops, then cut through the joint

quiz.q: What is the chicken oyster?
choices: A round pocket of meat on the back, kept with the thigh
quiz.explain: It's the best bite on the bird.

quiz.q: What marks the knee joint from the outside?
choices: A line of fat across the leg
quiz.explain: Cut straight down through the fat line.

knowledge.title: Yield and cost: a whole bird vs. parts
body: A whole chicken almost always costs less per pound than the same chicken sold in parts, because the store charges for the butchering. But some of a whole bird's weight is back, neck, and bone you won't serve. The question is what you pay per pound of what you actually eat.

Yield is the weight you use divided by the weight you bought. A 4-pound chicken usually gives about 2⅞ pounds of serving pieces (breasts, thighs, drumsticks, wings) and 1⅛ pounds of back, neck, and trim. That's a yield of about 72 percent.

Here's the math with sample prices; your store's will differ. A whole chicken at $1.50 a pound, 4 pounds, costs $6.00. Divided by the 2⅞ pounds of pieces, that's $2.09 a pound of serving pieces. Bought separately, bone-in thighs might be $2.00 a pound and breasts $4.00, a mix averaging around $2.95. The whole bird wins, and the back becomes free stock.
The break-even point is the parts price at which the whole bird stops saving money: whole-bird price divided by yield. If parts ever cost less than that, buy parts.
What the math leaves out: your time (about 5 minutes once you're practiced), freezer space, and whether your family eats every part. A whole bird pays only if nothing is wasted.
steps: Find today's prices at your store for a whole chicken, bone-in thighs, drumsticks, wings, and breasts.
Use your weights from the drill to work out your bird's yield and its cost per pound of serving pieces.
Work out the break-even parts price, and compare it with the store's.
Write two sentences: which was cheaper this week, and when you'd choose the other.

quiz.q: What is yield?
choices: The weight you use divided by the weight you bought

quiz.q: A 5-pound bird gives 3.6 pounds of pieces. What's the yield?
A whole bird costs $1.50 a pound with a 72% yield. What's the break-even parts price?
What does the yield math leave out?
choices: Your time, freezer space, and waste
quiz.explain: A bird only pays if every part is used.

sabbath.title: Freeze the back and wings for stock
body: The back, neck, and wing tips from a whole chicken are the start of a good stock: mostly bone and connective tissue, which is what gives stock its body. Saved in the freezer until there's enough, they cost nothing extra.
steps: Bag the back and wing tips from this week's chicken in a freezer bag. Press out the air.
Label the bag with the date and "chicken backs for stock." Keep a running count on the label as you add more.
Freeze it flat, so it stacks and thaws quickly. Use it within 3 months.
When you have the backs of 2 or 3 chickens (about 3 pounds), they're enough for about 3 quarts of stock: cover with cold water, add onion, carrot, celery, bay, and peppercorns, and simmer 3 hours.
Wash your hands and everything the raw chicken touched.

quiz.q: Why are backs good for stock?
choices: They're mostly bone and connective tissue, which give stock its body

quiz.q: How long do frozen backs keep?
Why freeze the bag flat?

drill.title: Trim silverskin; score duck skin
body: Two trims a restaurant prep cook does every day: taking silverskin off beef, and scoring duck skin so its fat renders. Do the one for the dish you're cooking this week on its own meat. For the other, watch a short video and practice the knife work on a vegetable, so you don't buy a second cut.
steps: If you're cooking the flank steak: lay it on the raw-meat board and find the thin, shiny membrane on its surface.
Slide the tip of a sharp, flexible knife under one end of it. Grip the freed tab with a paper towel.

Angle the blade slightly up, toward the membrane, and saw gently along under it while pulling the tab back. Take it off in strips, losing as little meat as you can. Weigh the trim and note it as a percentage of the steak.

If you're cooking the duck: lay a breast skin side up. With the tip of the knife, cut lines ⅜ inch apart diagonally across the skin, through the fat but not into the meat. Turn it and cut the other way, for diamonds. No red meat should show; if it does, cut shallower.
For the trim you aren't doing, watch a short video of it (search "remove silverskin from steak" or "score duck breast").

Then practice that motion on a vegetable: score a crosshatch through the skin of a halved eggplant or zucchini without cutting into the flesh, or slide the knife just under the peel of a cucumber, blade angled up, taking off a thin strip.
Refrigerate the meat for this week's recipe, use the vegetable in a stir-fry or salad, and wash your hands, the knife, and the board.

quiz.q: Which way does the blade angle when you remove silverskin?
quiz.explain: So you lose as little meat as possible.

quiz.q: How deep do you score duck skin?
choices: Through the skin and fat, not into the meat
Only the surface of the skin

quiz.q: Why remove silverskin?
choices: It tightens and turns rubbery when cooked

knowledge.title: Primal cuts and the method each suits
body: A beef carcass is first cut into large sections called primals, and each primal into the cuts you buy. Knowing which primal a cut comes from tells you how hard that muscle worked, and so how to cook it.

Chuck (the shoulder) works constantly: flavorful, full of connective tissue, and best braised or stewed (pot roast, stew meat, ground chuck). Rib and short loin (along the upper back) barely work: tender, marbled cuts for dry, fast heat (ribeye, strip, tenderloin). Sirloin, behind them, is a little firmer and still good seared or grilled. Round (the hind leg) is lean and tough unless sliced thin or braised. Brisket and plate (the chest and belly) are fatty and tough, made for long, slow cooking. Flank, below the loin, is lean and fibrous, with lots of flavor: seared hot, sliced thin across the grain.

The rule: muscles that move a lot are tough and suited to moist, slow heat (braising, stewing); muscles that move little are tender and suited to dry, fast heat (searing, grilling, roasting). Lamb follows the same map: shoulder and shank for braising, rack and loin for roasting.

Poultry follows it too. Legs work and are dark, rich, and forgiving; breasts are lean and dry quickly. Duck breast is darker than chicken breast because ducks fly: it's a working muscle, rich and red, and it slices like a steak.
steps: Draw a simple outline of a steer and divide it into the primals on this page: chuck, rib, short loin, sirloin, round, brisket, plate, flank.
On each, write one cut and one cooking method.
At a store or butcher, find three beef cuts. Write down each primal, its price per pound, and how you'd cook it.

quiz.q: Which primal is best for braising?
Why is flank sliced thin across the grain?
choices: It's lean and fibrous; short fibers are tender

quiz.q: Why is duck breast darker than chicken breast?
choices: Ducks fly, so the breast is a working muscle

quiz.q: Which method suits a tender cut like ribeye?
choices: Dry, fast heat: searing or grilling

sabbath.title: Clean birds: duck, goose, quail, and the birds Leviticus names (Leviticus 11:13–19)
body: Leviticus 11:13–19 lists the birds Israel was not to eat: the eagle, the vultures, the kite and falcon, every raven, the ostrich, the nighthawk and sea gull, the hawk, the owls, the cormorant, the stork, the heron, the hoopoe, and the bat. Most hunt or eat what's already dead. Deuteronomy 14:11–20 repeats the list and adds, "All clean winged things you may eat."

Every bird not on the list is clean. That includes the domestic birds raised for food (chicken, turkey, duck, goose) and many game birds: quail, pheasant, partridge, grouse, guinea fowl, and pigeon and dove. Scripture shows clean birds in use: turtledoves and pigeons as offerings (Leviticus 1:14; 12:8), and quail sent to Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13).
This week's duck and week 10's quail are both clean. Duck and goose are richer than chicken, with dark breast meat and a thick layer of fat under the skin, which is why they're scored and rendered.
steps: Read Leviticus 11:13–19 and Deuteronomy 14:11–20.
Sort these into clean and unclean using the passages: duck, goose, heron, quail, ostrich, pheasant, raven, turkey.
Look up the hoopoe and the cormorant. Write one sentence on what each eats.
Find duck, quail, or another game bird at a store or online. Write down the price per pound and compare it with chicken.

quiz.q: How does Leviticus 11 identify unclean birds?
Which of these is clean?
What does Deuteronomy 14:20 say?
choices: "All clean winged things you may eat"
quiz.explain: Every bird not listed is clean.

drill.title: Skin and portion a side of salmon; pull the pin bones
body: A whole side of salmon costs less per pound than portions, and portioning it yourself is quick once you've done it. If your family is cooking the teriyaki salmon side, this drill is its first steps. If you're cooking the veracruzana, don't buy a side for it: watch a fishmonger do it on video, then practice on one skin-on fillet.
steps: Cooking the veracruzana instead? Watch a short video of a side of salmon being skinned and portioned (search "how to portion a side of salmon"), then do the steps below on one skin-on salmon fillet, and cook it any way you like this week.
Lay the side skin down on the raw-meat board with the head end to your left (to your right if you're left-handed).
Run your fingertips along the thick half, from the head end toward the tail. Pull each pin bone with tweezers toward the head, at the angle it lies. Count them; a side usually has 25 to 35.
Turn the side so the tail points toward you. Cut down through the flesh to the skin about ¾ inch from the tail end.
Grip the tail flap of skin with a paper towel. Hold the knife nearly flat against the skin, and pull the skin toward you in small side-to-side movements while the knife stays almost still.
Trim off the thin belly fat along the bottom edge and any brown flesh on the skinned side.
Portion by weight: about 5 ounces each. Cut the thick head end into narrower pieces and the tail into wider ones, folding the thinnest tail under.
Weigh the trim and the skin. Note the yield.
Wash the knife, tweezers, board, and your hands with hot, soapy water.

quiz.q: How do you hold the knife when skinning?
choices: Nearly flat against the skin, almost still, while you pull the skin

quiz.q: How do you portion a side evenly?
choices: By weight, narrower at the thick end and wider at the tail

quiz.q: About how many pin bones does a side of salmon have?
quiz.explain: They run along the thick half.

knowledge.title: Buying fish: wild and farmed, labels, questions for the fish counter
body: Every fish sold at a U.S. counter must be labeled with its name, where it came from, and whether it was wild-caught or farm-raised. Those three things, plus a few questions, tell you most of what you need.

Name. On a fillet or steak you can't see the scales, so the name is how you know a fish is clean (fins and scales, Leviticus 11:9). Watch for vague names. "Snapper" sold in some places covers several kinds; "red snapper" is one species. Fish that are commonly substituted include snapper, grouper, and cod. If a name is vague or the price is far below other stores, ask.

Wild or farmed. Wild salmon is leaner, deeper in color, and seasonal; farmed salmon is fattier, milder, and steady in price and supply. Both are clean. Farmed fish vary with how they're raised; certification labels from independent groups tell you a farm meets set standards for feed, crowding, and the water around it.

Fresh, frozen, and "previously frozen." Fish frozen at sea within hours of the catch is often better than "fresh" fish that's been on ice for a week. "Previously frozen" at the counter means it was thawed for display: cook it within a day and don't refreeze it.
Questions for the fish counter: What is it, exactly? Where's it from? When did it come in? Was it frozen? Can I smell it? Will you scale and gut it, or skin it?
steps: At a fish counter, read the labels on four fish. Write down each one's name, origin, and wild or farmed.
Ask two of the questions on this page, and write down the answers.
Compare the price per pound of a side of salmon with salmon portions. Using your drill yield, work out the real cost of the side per pound of portions.

quiz.q: What three things must a U.S. fish label show?
choices: Its name, where it's from, and wild or farmed

quiz.q: What does "previously frozen" mean at the counter?
choices: It was thawed for display: cook within a day, don't refreeze
quiz.explain: Thawed fish has a short clock.

quiz.q: Why does the fish's name matter most?
choices: Without the skin, it's how you know the fish has fins and scales
It tells you how to cook it

quiz.q: A label says "snapper." What do you do?
choices: Ask which kind, and whether it's red snapper
quiz.explain: Snapper is a name some stores use loosely.

sabbath.title: Fins and scales, and the fishermen Jesus called (Leviticus 11:9–12; Luke 5:1–11)
body: "These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat" (Leviticus 11:9). The rule is repeated in Deuteronomy 14:9–10.

In Luke 5:1–11, Jesus borrows Simon Peter's boat to teach the crowd from the water. Afterward He tells Peter to put out into deep water and let down the nets. Peter answers, "Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets" (Luke 5:5). The catch is so large the nets begin to break and two boats nearly sink.
Peter falls at Jesus' knees. Jesus tells him, "Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men" (Luke 5:10). They brought their boats to land, left everything, and followed Him (Luke 5:11).
The disciples' trade was the fish of the Sea of Galilee, sold in the markets and salted for the cities, and the Gospels return to those boats and nets again and again.
steps: Read Leviticus 11:9–12 and Luke 5:1–11.
Answer in writing: what did Peter's answer in Luke 5:5 show about him?
Answer in writing: what did the fishermen leave behind in Luke 5:11, and what would that have meant for their families' living?
Find two more Gospel passages where Jesus meets His disciples at their boats or eats fish with them (start with Mark 1:16–20 and John 21).

choices: "At your word I will let down the nets"

quiz.q: What happened to the nets?
choices: They began to break from the catch
